These findings highlight the importance of exploring the full representational depth of molecular encoders to achieve substantial performance improvements and computational efficiency. The code will be made publicly available.

papers.title: Scalable Mechanistic Neural Networks for Differential Equations and Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we reformulate the Mechanistic Neural Network to achieve linear time and space complexity with respect to sequence length while maintaining accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces S-MNN, a reformulation of the Mechanistic Neural Network that reduces computational time and space complexities from cubic/quadratic to linear in sequence length while maintaining accuracy.
papers.conclusion: S-MNN addresses the scalability limitations of MNN by reducing complexities to linear in sequence length, retaining precision and enabling efficient modeling of long-term dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
S-MNN matches the precision of the original MNN across various benchmarks.
S-MNN reduces computational time and memory usage significantly, enabling handling of long sequences.
The reformulation eliminates slack variables and uses a banded matrix structure for efficient solving.
S-MNN demonstrates practical applicability on long-term climate data forecasting.
The solver is numerically stable and GPU-friendly, achieving linear scaling in time and memory.
papers.abstract: We propose Scalable Mechanistic Neural Network (S-MNN), an enhanced neural network framework designed for scientific machine learning applications involving long temporal sequences. By reformulating the original Mechanistic Neural Network (MNN) (Pervez et al., 2024), we reduce the computational time and space complexities from cubic and quadratic with respect to the sequence length, respectively, to linear. This significant improvement enables efficient modeling of long-term dynamics without sacrificing accuracy or interpretability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that S-MNN matches the original MNN in precision while substantially reducing computational resources. Consequently, S-MNN can drop-in replace the original MNN in applications, providing a practical and efficient tool for integrating mechanistic bottlenecks into neural network models of complex dynamical systems. Source code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/ScalableMNN.

papers.title: Exploiting Latent Linearity in LLMs Improves Explainable Molecular Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can LLM-derived molecular representations be linearly decomposed into chemically meaningful concepts (functional groups), and how can this latent linearity be exploited for explainable molecular property prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MoleX, a framework that decomposes LLM latent representations into a concept-aligned space of functional groups and shows that a sparse linear mapping onto these chemical concepts improves both predictive accuracy and explainability for molecular property prediction.
papers.conclusion: Exploiting latent linearity in LLM representations provides a principled basis for effective and explainable molecular representation learning, improving accuracy, explainability, and efficiency in molecular property prediction.
papers.key_findings:
LLM-derived molecular representations exhibit latent linearity that can be expressed as a weighted combination of chemically meaningful functional group concepts.
MoleX outperforms existing GNN, LLM, and explainable machine learning baselines in predictive accuracy and explanation faithfulness on benchmark molecular property prediction tasks.
A residual calibration strategy corrects errors from the base linear predictor, further improving accuracy and explanation alignment with ground-truth substructures.
MoleX achieves significant computational efficiency, with CPU inference over 300x faster than LLMs and using 100,000 fewer parameters.
The linear predictor's performance scales with model size, training precision, and dataset size, but task-adapted training is crucial for converting capacity into performance gains.
papers.limitation: The linear predictor may underfit complex molecular patterns in some cases, as there is a trade-off between model complexity and performance.
future_direction: Examine the complexity–performance trade-off in LLM-based molecular representation learning to identify optimal balances between model complexity and downstream performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated broad utility across molecular domains, spanning drug discovery and materials design. Analyzing LLMs' latent representations is crucial for elucidating their underlying mechanisms, improving explainability, and ultimately advancing downstream performance. We propose MoleX, a simple yet effective framework that decomposes molecular embeddings within LLM representations into a concept-aligned space for explainable molecular representation learning. We further show that these high-dimensional embeddings admit a linear mapping onto chemically consistent concepts. Our analysis suggests that the uncovered linearity aligns with established chemical principles, indicating a mechanistically explainable latent structure in LLM representations for scientific applications. When applied to downstream tasks, this latent linearity improves both predictive and explanatory performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MoleX outperforms existing approaches in accuracy, explainability, and efficiency, achieving CPU inference on large-scale datasets 300 times faster with 100,000 fewer parameters than LLMs.

papers.title: An introduction to graphical tensor notation for mechanistic interpretability
papers.core_contribution: Introduces graphical tensor notation as a tool for understanding and communicating mechanistic interpretability results, especially for tensor operations in neural networks like transformers.
papers.conclusion: Graphical tensor notation is a useful tool for understanding and communicating interpretability results, especially for operations involving many tensors, and it surfaces dualities and equivalences more easily than other notations.
papers.key_findings:
Graphical tensor notation simplifies the representation of tensor operations, making it easier to parse complex computations and see equivalences.
The notation can be applied to decompose tensors (e.g., SVD, CP, Tucker) and to represent neural network components, including transformers.
The paper demonstrates how to represent transformer components (embedding, MLP, attention) and the residual stream using graphical notation.
It shows how to construct a toy induction head circuit using graphical tensor notation, illustrating how attention heads can compose across layers.
Graphical notation helps in expanding the computation of a transformer into a sum of paths, which can aid in interpretability by isolating important terms.
papers.abstract: Graphical tensor notation is a simple way of denoting linear operations on tensors, originating from physics. Modern deep learning consists almost entirely of operations on or between tensors, so easily understanding tensor operations is quite important for understanding these systems. This is especially true when attempting to reverse-engineer the algorithms learned by a neural network in order to understand its behavior: a field known as mechanistic interpretability. It's often easy to get confused about which operations are happening between tensors and lose sight of the overall structure, but graphical tensor notation makes it easier to parse things at a glance and see interesting equivalences. The first half of this document introduces the notation and applies it to some decompositions (SVD, CP, Tucker, and tensor network decompositions), while the second half applies it to some existing some foundational approaches for mechanistically understanding language models, loosely following ``A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits'', then constructing an example ``induction head'' circuit in graphical tensor notation.

papers.title: Maximum entropy methods for extracting the learned features of deep neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we interpret deep neural networks and extract the features they learn from input data using maximum entropy methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a maximum entropy method for interpreting deep neural networks by sampling sequences that preserve penultimate layer activations, allowing extraction of learned features such as motifs and nucleosome positioning signals.
papers.conclusion: The maximum entropy method provides a valuable tool for interpreting deep neural networks, particularly in biological sequence analysis, and demonstrates synergy between statistical physics and machine learning for extracting subtle sequence features.
papers.key_findings:
The MaxEnt method successfully captures XOR logic learned by a simple ANN, while Saliency Map and DeepLIFT methods fail to do so.
The MaxEnt method localizes CTCF binding motifs with better agreement with conventional motif discovery tools (MEME/FIMO) than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The MaxEnt method extracts nucleosome positioning signals, including periodic GC content at 10 bp intervals, more effectively than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The method can assess the importance of global sequence features (e.g., GC content) via a feature importance score derived from the variance of MCMC samples.
Features extracted by MaxEnt (low-variance principal components) can be used for classification, as demonstrated by a nearest neighbor classifier achieving 76% accuracy.
papers.limitation: The MaxEnt method is computationally expensive compared to Saliency Map and DeepLIFT due to MCMC sampling.
papers.abstract: New architectures of multilayer artificial neural networks and new methods for training them are rapidly revolutionizing the application of machine learning in diverse fields, including business, social science, physical sciences, and biology. Interpreting deep neural networks, however, currently remains elusive, and a critical challenge lies in understanding which meaningful features a network is actually learning. We present a general method for interpreting deep neural networks and extracting network-learned features from input data. We describe our algorithm in the context of biological sequence analysis. Our approach, based on ideas from statistical physics, samples from the maximum entropy distribution over possible sequences, anchored at an input sequence and subject to constraints implied by the empirical function learned by a network. Using our framework, we demonstrate that local transcription factor binding motifs can be identified from a network trained on ChIP-seq data and that nucleosome positioning signals are indeed learned by a network trained on chemical cleavage nucleosome maps. Imposing a further constraint on the maximum entropy distribution also allows us to probe whether a network is learning global sequence features, such as the high GC content in nucleosome-rich regions. This work thus provides valuable mathematical tools for interpreting and extracting learned features from feed-forward neural networks.

papers.title: Prototype-Based Interpretable Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can prototype-based interpretable networks (ProtoPNet and TesNet) be adapted to the graph domain for graph and node classification, and do these adapted models provide interpretability while maintaining or improving performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts prototype-based interpretable networks (ProtoPNet and TesNet) to graph neural networks, demonstrating that these models can achieve equal or better classification performance than black-box counterparts while providing intrinsic interpretability through prototype activations.
papers.conclusion: Prototype-based models can be successfully adapted to the graph domain for interpretable graph and node classification, providing a basis for future development of interpretable graph neural network architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Adapted ProtoPNet and TesNet models, especially TesNet with GIN backbone, often outperform their black-box counterparts on graph and node classification tasks.
The proposed k-hop method for visualizing prototype activations provides clearer explanations without sacrificing fidelity.
The interpretable models produce more faithful explanations (higher Fidelity+) than post-hoc methods and other self-explainable models like ProtGNN and SEGNN.
Transfer learning does not provide advantages in this setting, likely due to differences in graph domains (domain of applicability).
The number of prototypes per class is a hyperparameter that requires tuning, but no general pattern was found across datasets.
papers.limitation:
Transfer learning does not work well due to differences in graph domains (domain of applicability).
The number of prototypes is a hyperparameter that needs to be tuned.
future_direction: Investigate the use of metrics better tailored to the graph domain.
Develop methods to automatically modulate the number of prototypes learned by the model.
Further development of interpretable graph architectures.
papers.abstract: Graph neural networks have proved to be a key tool for dealing with many problems and domains such as chemistry, natural language processing and social networks. While the structure of the layers is simple, it is difficult to identify the patterns learned by the graph neural network. Several works propose post-hoc methods to explain graph predictions, but few of them try to generate interpretable models. Conversely, the topic of the interpretable models is highly investigated in image recognition. Given the similarity between image and graph domains, we analyze the adaptability of prototype-based neural networks for graph and node classification. In particular, we investigate the use of two interpretable networks, ProtoPNet and TesNet, in the graph domain. We show that the adapted networks manage to reach better or higher accuracy scores than their respective black-box models and comparable performances with state-of-the-art self-explainable models. Showing how to extract ProtoPNet and TesNet explanations on graph neural networks, we further study how to obtain global and local explanations for the trained models. We then evaluate the explanations of the interpretable models by comparing them with post-hoc approaches and self-explainable models. Our findings show that the application of TesNet and ProtoPNet to the graph domain produces qualitative predictions while improving their reliability and transparency.

papers.title: A technical note on bilinear layers for interpretability
papers.research_question: Can bilinear layers, which are mathematically simpler than standard MLPs, enable better mechanistic interpretability by allowing formal analysis of circuits and feature construction?
papers.core_contribution: Bilinear layers can be expressed using only linear operations and third-order tensors, enabling extension of the mathematical framework for transformer circuits to include MLP layers and offering a path to interpret feature construction via additive pairwise nonlinear interactions.
papers.conclusion: Bilinear layers are mathematically simpler to analyze than standard MLPs, potentially enabling formal analysis of circuits in transformers with MLPs and offering a path to understand feature construction mechanisms in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Bilinear layers can be expressed using only linear operations and third-order tensors.
This expression allows extending the mathematical framework for transformer circuits (previously limited to attention-only transformers) to transformers with MLP layers.
Bilinear layers are additively pairwise nonlinear, meaning output features are constructed through sums of pairwise interactions between input features, unlike standard MLPs which are fully nonlinear.
The additive pairwise structure makes feature construction in bilinear layers more decomposable and potentially easier to interpret.
The paper provides a mathematical expression for a one-layer transformer with bilinear MLPs.
papers.limitation:
It remains to be determined whether bilinear layers continue to perform competitively at larger scales.
The approach to understanding feature construction in bilinear layers is speculative and requires empirical validation.
future_direction: Analyzing learning dynamics of bilinear layers.
Empirical evaluation of feature construction in bilinear networks.
Extending the mathematical framework to multi-layer transformers.
papers.abstract: The ability of neural networks to represent more features than neurons makes interpreting them challenging. This phenomenon, known as superposition, has spurred efforts to find architectures that are more interpretable than standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) with elementwise activation functions. In this note, I examine bilinear layers, which are a type of MLP layer that are mathematically much easier to analyze while simultaneously performing better than standard MLPs. Although they are nonlinear functions of their input, I demonstrate that bilinear layers can be expressed using only linear operations and third order tensors. We can integrate this expression for bilinear layers into a mathematical framework for transformer circuits, which was previously limited to attention-only transformers. These results suggest that bilinear layers are easier to analyze mathematically than current architectures and thus may lend themselves to deeper safety insights by allowing us to talk more formally about circuits in neural networks. Additionally, bilinear layers may offer an alternative path for mechanistic interpretability through understanding the mechanisms of feature construction instead of enumerating a (potentially exponentially) large number of features in large models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Binary and Ternary Transformers
papers.research_question: Do binary and ternary transformer networks learn distinctly different or similar algorithms compared to full-precision transformer networks for modular addition?
papers.core_contribution: Binary and ternary transformers learn similar Fourier-based algorithms as full-precision transformers for modular addition, providing evidence against their use as more interpretable alternatives.
papers.conclusion: Binary and ternary transformers learn similar algorithms to full-precision transformers for modular addition and are not more interpretable, with binary models showing more noise in analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Binary and ternary networks exhibit grokking behavior similar to full-precision networks when weight decay regularization is applied.
Binary and ternary models learn similar periodic patterns in embeddings and logits as full-precision models.
Binary models show more noise in Fourier analysis compared to full-precision models.
Ternary models behave intermediately between binary and full-precision models but do not achieve superior loss.
No evidence was found that binary or ternary networks learn simpler, more interpretable discrete algorithms.
papers.limitation:
Lack of conclusive evidence concerning exactly what algorithm was learned, since many different algorithms could be learned for modular addition.
The implementation did not binarize/ternarize the embed and unembed layers, limiting the study to partially binarized networks.
Only the most basic straight-through estimator technique was explored for optimizing binary/ternary networks.
future_direction: Explore more complicated techniques for optimizing binary and ternary networks using mechanistic interpretability.
Investigate fully binarized/ternarized networks in all layers.
Investigate whether binary and ternary networks always learn similar algorithms for other toy problems or in language models.
papers.abstract: Recent research (arXiv:2310.11453, arXiv:2402.17764) has proposed binary and ternary transformer networks as a way to significantly reduce memory and improve inference speed in Large Language Models (LLMs) while maintaining accuracy. In this work, we apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to investigate whether such networks learn distinctly different or similar algorithms when compared to full-precision transformer networks. In particular, we reverse engineer the algorithms learned for the toy problem of modular addition where we find that binary and ternary networks learn similar algorithms as full precision networks. This provides evidence against the possibility of using binary and ternary networks as a more interpretable alternative in the LLM setting.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: Explainable Molecular Property Prediction: Aligning Chemical Concepts with Predictions via Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we provide chemically meaningful and faithful explanations for molecular property predictions using language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Lamole, a framework for explainable molecular property prediction that uses Group SELFIES representation and combines attention weights with gradients, calibrated by a marginal loss, to provide chemically meaningful and faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: Lamole provides chemically meaningful and faithful explanations for molecular property prediction and can be integrated into an interpretable optimization pipeline for molecular design.
papers.key_findings:
Lamole achieves prediction accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art baselines while improving explanation accuracy by up to 14.3%.
The proposed information flow-based explanation method, integrating attention and gradients, captures interactions between functional groups.
The marginal loss aligns explanations with the tangent space of the data manifold, ensuring concept-aligned results.
Using only 10% of molecules with ground truth annotations can significantly improve explanation accuracy.
Integration with an evolutionary algorithm demonstrates Lamole's actionable utility for guiding molecular editing and optimization.
papers.limitation:
Complex interactions caused by multiple functional groups may not be fully captured, and other functional groups may receive relatively high importance scores.
The molecular editing case is a computational demonstration and does not imply real-world chemical optimality.
future_direction: Extending the framework to broader generalization scenarios, including unseen chemotypes.
Designing more strategies to reveal complex functional group interactions.
papers.abstract: Providing explainable molecular property predictions is critical for many scientific domains, such as drug discovery and material science. Though transformer-based language models have shown great potential in accurate molecular property prediction, they neither provide chemically meaningful explanations nor faithfully reveal the molecular structure-property relationships. In this work, we develop a framework for explainable molecular property prediction based on language models, dubbed as Lamole, which can provide chemical concepts-aligned explanations. We take a string-based molecular representation -- Group SELFIES -- as input tokens to pretrain and fine-tune our Lamole, as it provides chemically meaningful semantics. By disentangling the information flows of Lamole, we propose combining self-attention weights and gradients for better quantification of each chemically meaningful substructure's impact on the model's output. To make the explanations more faithfully respect the structure-property relationship, we then carefully craft a marginal loss to explicitly optimize the explanations to be able to align with the chemists' annotations. We bridge the manifold hypothesis with the elaborated marginal loss to prove that the loss can align the explanations with the tangent space of the data manifold, leading to concept-aligned explanations. Experimental results over six mutagenicity datasets and one hepatotoxicity dataset demonstrate Lamole can achieve comparable classification accuracy and boost the explanation accuracy by up to 14.3%, being the state-of-the-art in explainable molecular property prediction.

papers.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably re-discover known algorithms for solving those tasks, and under what conditions do they discover familiar algorithmic solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on modular addition can discover qualitatively different algorithms (Clock, Pizza, and others), with the algorithm learned depending on hyperparameters like attention rate and width, revealing algorithmic phase transitions and the need for tools to characterize algorithmic phase spaces.
papers.conclusion: Algorithmic discoveries in neural networks are not inevitable; even simple tasks admit a diversity of solutions, motivating the development of tools to characterize the algorithmic phase space of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Networks can learn either the previously described Clock algorithm or a new, less intuitive Pizza algorithm for modular addition.
The Pizza algorithm uses averaging and absolute value operations, while the Clock algorithm uses multiplication via attention.
Models sometimes implement multiple, parallel copies of an algorithm (ensembling) for robustness.
Sharp algorithmic phase transitions between Clock and Pizza occur as model hyperparameters (attention rate, width) are varied.
Non-circular algorithms also exist, especially in deeper networks or with low attention rates.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a single learning problem (modular addition), and scaling the techniques to more complex models and real-world tasks requires significant additional work.
future_direction: How to find, classify, and interpret unfamiliar algorithms in a systematic way.
How to disentangle multiple, parallel algorithm implementations in the presence of ensembling.
papers.abstract: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably rediscover known algorithms for solving those tasks? Several recent studies, on tasks ranging from group arithmetic to in-context linear regression, have suggested that the answer is yes. Using modular addition as a prototypical problem, we show that algorithm discovery in neural networks is sometimes more complex. Small changes to model hyperparameters and initializations can induce the discovery of qualitatively different algorithms from a fixed training set, and even parallel implementations of multiple such algorithms. Some networks trained to perform modular addition implement a familiar Clock algorithm; others implement a previously undescribed, less intuitive, but comprehensible procedure which we term the Pizza algorithm, or a variety of even more complex procedures. Our results show that even simple learning problems can admit a surprising diversity of solutions, motivating the development of new tools for characterizing the behavior of neural networks across their algorithmic phase space.

papers.title: Occupancies vs Embeddings: Internal representations of Ab Initio and Graph Probabilistic Models*
papers.research_question: To what degree does the end-to-end data-driven approach (graph neural networks) coalesce with traditional ab initio predictions of molecular behavior? Does the model contain internal characteristics of the wave function or electron density from DFT?
papers.core_contribution: This study compares atomwise representations from graph neural networks (GNNs) and ab initio density functional theory (DFT), revealing that GNN embeddings offer higher resolution and can accurately predict DFT-derived atomic occupancy values, whereas the reverse mapping is significantly less accurate.
papers.conclusion: GNN embeddings serve as a richer, more informative molecular representation than DFT-derived atomic occupancies, demonstrating the power of end-to-end statistical models to encapsulate and extend traditional quantum chemical information, though further exploration is needed regarding their robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.key_findings:
Both GNN embedding vectors and DFT-derived atomic occupancy vectors can separate and label chemical environments, but embeddings provide much higher resolution and lower classification error.
Embedding vectors can predict atomic occupancy values with high accuracy (MAE 2.5e-3, R2 0.996), but the reverse mapping from occupancies to embeddings is an order of magnitude less accurate (MAE 0.235, R2 0.379).
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reveals qualitative similarities in the eigenvalue spectra between the two representations, but the embedding space captures more nuanced information.
The embedding representation contains more information than the occupancy representation, enabling precise mapping to occupancies but not vice versa within the same model chemistry.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) shows embeddings achieve near-perfect functional group classification, while occupancy vectors show higher error, especially for similar chemical environments.
papers.limitation: Interatomic information was omitted due to the need to respect rotational equivariance for the embeddings, and the use of Mulliken population analysis might hamper a faithful analysis of the information content in the occupancies.
future_direction: Further studies to tighten conclusions about the relationship between embeddings and electron density.
Exploration of GNN embeddings' robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical modeling has traditionally been separated into two fairly non-overlapping frameworks: the exact framework of \textit{ab initio} models and the data-driven framework of statistical models. However, recent advances in machine learning approaches have intercepted the exact \textit{ab initio} frameworks by using an \textit{end-to-end} probabilistic model of the Schr\"odinger equation in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation---from raw nuclear configurations to quantum observables such as the energy. While probabilistic modelling offers promising advancements to speed up computational predictions, the internal representation and its connection to the underlying quantum data---the wave function or electron density---which they implicitly rely on for training, remains relatively poorly understood. This study seeks to make a first comparison of the internal representation from a probabilistic end-to-end models with those from pure \textit{ab initio} frameworks such as density functional theory. We do this by comparing the internal atomwise representation of graph models, also called embeddings, to their most natural \textit{ab initio} counterpart, electron occupancy values. Our findings show that the embedding representations can be employed to transfer learn atomic occupancy values whereas the reverse mapping appears to be less accurate. We discuss the assumption that the probabilistic model could infer the existence of an underlying electron density underpinning the computational \textit{ab-initio} data.

papers.title: Beyond Components: Singular Vector-Based Interpretability of Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: Can transformer components (attention heads and MLPs) be decomposed into orthogonal singular directions that reveal superposed and independent computations within a single head or MLP?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a directional interpretability perspective that decomposes transformer components into orthogonal singular directions, showing that multiple low-rank, interpretable computations coexist within single attention heads and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transformer computations are more distributed, structured, and compositional than previously assumed, opening new avenues for fine-grained mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of learned singular directions can faithfully preserve model behavior.
These directions align with meaningful subfunctions, e.g., in IOI, name mover heads encode multiple overlapping subfunctions along distinct singular directions.
Components identified as part of known circuits exhibit strong engagement along specific singular directions, indicating computations are embedded in compact subspaces.
Transformer computations are distributed, structured, and compositional, with overlapping subfunctions embedded within shared subspaces.
Singular directions can be used for controlled interventions, e.g., in gender pronoun resolution, scaling directions can modify predictions.
papers.limitation: Some directions remain challenging to interpret fully.
future_direction: Conduct targeted intervention experiments to validate causal contributions of discovered components.
Examine whether these mechanisms generalize to larger or more capable models (e.g., Phi, LLaMA).
Explore activation of these mechanisms in real-world settings.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit complex and distributed behavior, yet their internal computations remain poorly understood. Existing mechanistic interpretability methods typically treat attention heads and multilayer perceptron layers (MLPs) (the building blocks of a transformer architecture) as indivisible units, overlooking possibilities of functional substructure learned within them. In this work, we introduce a more fine-grained perspective that decomposes these components into orthogonal singular directions, revealing superposed and independent computations within a single head or MLP. We validate our perspective on widely used standard tasks like Indirect Object Identification (IOI), Gender Pronoun (GP), and Greater Than (GT), showing that previously identified canonical functional heads, such as the name mover, encode multiple overlapping subfunctions aligned with distinct singular directions. Nodes in a computational graph, that are previously identified as circuit elements show strong activation along specific low-rank directions, suggesting that meaningful computations reside in compact subspaces. While some directions remain challenging to interpret fully, our results highlight that transformer computations are more distributed, structured, and compositional than previously assumed. This perspective opens new avenues for fine-grained mechanistic interpretability and a deeper understanding of model internals.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Transformers are efficient hierarchical chemical graph learners
papers.research_question: How can we design an efficient graph transformer that reduces computational cost and captures long-range interactions in molecular graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SubFormer, a graph transformer that combines hierarchical clustering and message-passing to efficiently learn graph representations, reducing computational cost and capturing long-range interactions while being competitive with state-of-the-art methods.
papers.conclusion: SubFormer performed consistently well on standard benchmarks for predicting molecular properties from chemical structures. Visualization of the attention maps suggests the model learns chemically pertinent features. SubFormer does not suffer from over-squashing, but over-smoothing remains an issue requiring further study.
papers.key_findings:
SubFormer is competitive with state-of-the-art graph transformers on molecular property prediction benchmarks at a fraction of the computational cost.
SubFormer attention weights correspond to chemically meaningful fragments (e.g., aromatic rings, charge-transfer fragments).
SubFormer does not suffer from over-squashing because attention allows direct long-range interactions.
SubFormer exhibits limited over-smoothing compared to GAT, but still experiences over-smoothing with increasing layers.
SubFormer is more expressive than the 1-WL test for graph isomorphism.
papers.limitation: Over-smoothing remains an issue, demanding further study.
future_direction: Further study to address over-smoothing.
Refine the graph decomposition strategy to improve separation power.
papers.abstract: Transformers, adapted from natural language processing, are emerging as a leading approach for graph representation learning. Contemporary graph transformers often treat nodes or edges as separate tokens. This approach leads to computational challenges for even moderately-sized graphs due to the quadratic scaling of self-attention complexity with token count. In this paper, we introduce SubFormer, a graph transformer that operates on subgraphs that aggregate information by a message-passing mechanism. This approach reduces the number of tokens and enhances learning long-range interactions. We demonstrate SubFormer on benchmarks for predicting molecular properties from chemical structures and show that it is competitive with state-of-the-art graph transformers at a fraction of the computational cost, with training times on the order of minutes on a consumer-grade graphics card. We interpret the attention weights in terms of chemical structures. We show that SubFormer exhibits limited over-smoothing and avoids over-squashing, which is prevalent in traditional graph neural networks.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 Predict Acronyms? Extracting and Understanding a Circuit via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 Small perform the task of predicting three-letter acronyms, and what is the underlying circuit responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: This paper discovers and interprets the circuit responsible for three-letter acronym prediction in GPT-2 Small, identifying 8 key attention heads that copy information from words to acronym letters and showing that positional information is derived from attention patterns via the causal mask.
papers.conclusion: This work successfully identifies and interprets the circuit for three-letter acronym prediction in GPT-2 Small, laying the foundation for understanding more complex behaviors involving multiple consecutive token predictions via mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for three-letter acronym prediction in GPT-2 Small is composed of 8 attention heads (~5% of total heads), classified into three groups based on their role.
The circuit is sufficient for the task; ablating all other components preserves and even slightly improves performance.
The main components, termed 'letter mover heads' (8.11, 10.10, 9.9, 11.4), attend from the previous acronym letter position to the capital letter of the corresponding word and copy its content.
Letter mover heads use positional information derived from attention patterns (specifically attention paid to the BOS token due to the causal mask) rather than from positional embeddings.
The information flow for acronym prediction uses two paths: a direct path from the previous predicted letter and a fainter path from the previous word's capital letter via 'previous token heads'.
future_direction: Understanding more complex behaviors that involve predicting multiple tokens.
Further study of heads that contribute positively (potentially negative name mover heads) in the positional information experiments.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models are treated as black-boxes because of their large number of parameters and complex internal interactions, which is a serious safety concern. Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) intends to reverse-engineer neural network behaviors in terms of human-understandable components. In this work, we focus on understanding how GPT-2 Small performs the task of predicting three-letter acronyms. Previous works in the MI field have focused so far on tasks that predict a single token. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that tries to mechanistically understand a behavior involving the prediction of multiple consecutive tokens. We discover that the prediction is performed by a circuit composed of 8 attention heads (~5% of the total heads) which we classified in three groups according to their role. We also demonstrate that these heads concentrate the acronym prediction functionality. In addition, we mechanistically interpret the most relevant heads of the circuit and find out that they use positional information which is propagated via the causal mask mechanism. We expect this work to lay the foundation for understanding more complex behaviors involving multiple-token predictions.

papers.title: The Non-Linear Representation Dilemma: Is Causal Abstraction Enough for Mechanistic Interpretability?
papers.research_question: Is causal abstraction sufficient for mechanistic interpretability when alignment maps are not constrained to be linear?
papers.core_contribution: Causal abstraction becomes vacuous when alignment maps are allowed to be arbitrarily complex, leading to the non-linear representation dilemma where there is no principled way to balance map complexity and accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Causal abstraction is not enough for mechanistic interpretability without assumptions about how models encode information.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretically, any algorithm can be perfectly mapped to any neural network under reasonable assumptions if alignment maps are arbitrarily complex.
Empirically, non-linear alignment maps can achieve near-perfect interchange intervention accuracy even on randomly initialized models that do not solve the task.
The complexity of alignment maps needed to achieve perfect IIA decreases as the model trains.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical result relies on assumptions such as input-injectivity and output-surjectivity of the neural network.
Empirical alignment map training can suffer from grokking and requires careful hyperparameter tuning.
future_direction: Studying the connection between information-encoding assumptions and causal abstraction.
papers.abstract: The concept of causal abstraction got recently popularised to demystify the opaque decision-making processes of machine learning models; in short, a neural network can be abstracted as a higher-level algorithm if there exists a function which allows us to map between them. Notably, most interpretability papers implement these maps as linear functions, motivated by the linear representation hypothesis: the idea that features are encoded linearly in a model's representations. However, this linearity constraint is not required by the definition of causal abstraction. In this work, we critically examine the concept of causal abstraction by considering arbitrarily powerful alignment maps. In particular, we prove that under reasonable assumptions, any neural network can be mapped to any algorithm, rendering this unrestricted notion of causal abstraction trivial and uninformative. We complement these theoretical findings with empirical evidence, demonstrating that it is possible to perfectly map models to algorithms even when these models are incapable of solving the actual task; e.g., on an experiment using randomly initialised language models, our alignment maps reach 100\% interchange-intervention accuracy on the indirect object identification task. This raises the non-linear representation dilemma: if we lift the linearity constraint imposed to alignment maps in causal abstraction analyses, we are left with no principled way to balance the inherent trade-off between these maps' complexity and accuracy. Together, these results suggest an answer to our title's question: causal abstraction is not enough for mechanistic interpretability, as it becomes vacuous without assumptions about how models encode information. Studying the connection between this information-encoding assumption and causal abstraction should lead to exciting future work.

papers.title: Concept Bottleneck Language Models For protein design
papers.research_question: How can we design a protein language model that is controllable, interpretable, and debuggable without sacrificing performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Bottleneck Language Models, a novel architecture that incorporates human-understandable concepts via a concept bottleneck layer, enabling precise control, interpretability, and debugging while maintaining performance comparable to traditional language models.
papers.conclusion: CB-pLM provides a framework for controllable, interpretable, and debuggable language models without sacrificing performance, making it particularly valuable for high-stakes domains like protein design.
papers.key_findings:
CB-pLM achieves 3x better control in terms of change in concept magnitude and 16% improvement in control accuracy compared to baselines.
CB-pLM maintains pre-training perplexity and downstream task performance comparable to traditional masked protein language models.
CB-pLM enables multi-concept interventions with high accuracy (94% control accuracy).
CB-pLM allows interpretability and debugging by inspecting the linear decoder weights, revealing concept-token relationships.
CB-pLM can generalize to unseen concept combinations, as demonstrated on ColorMNIST.
future_direction: Extending CB-LM to other domains and architectures
Adding new concepts to a trained CB-LM via fine-tuning
Generalization to new concept combinations
papers.abstract: We introduce Concept Bottleneck Protein Language Models (CB-pLM), a generative masked language model with a layer where each neuron corresponds to an interpretable concept. Our architecture offers three key benefits: i) Control: We can intervene on concept values to precisely control the properties of generated proteins, achieving a 3 times larger change in desired concept values compared to baselines. ii) Interpretability: A linear mapping between concept values and predicted tokens allows transparent analysis of the model's decision-making process. iii) Debugging: This transparency facilitates easy debugging of trained models. Our models achieve pre-training perplexity and downstream task performance comparable to traditional masked protein language models, demonstrating that interpretability does not compromise performance. While adaptable to any language model, we focus on masked protein language models due to their importance in drug discovery and the ability to validate our model's capabilities through real-world experiments and expert knowledge. We scale our CB-pLM from 24 million to 3 billion parameters, making them the largest Concept Bottleneck Models trained and the first capable of generative language modeling.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: Circuit Insights: Towards Interpretability Beyond Activations
papers.research_question: How can we move beyond activation-based interpretability by using weight-based and circuit-based analysis to understand model computations, removing dependence on explainer LLMs and datasets?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces WeightLens and CircuitLens, two complementary methods for automated interpretability that go beyond activation analysis by using model weights and circuit-level dynamics, reducing dependence on external LLMs and datasets.
papers.conclusion: WeightLens and CircuitLens advance automated interpretability by moving beyond activations, providing more robust and scalable circuit analysis while maintaining efficiency and quality.
papers.key_findings:
WeightLens matches or exceeds activation-based methods for token-based features without needing explainer LLMs or datasets.
CircuitLens captures context-dependent features and circuit-level dynamics that activation-only methods miss.
Combining weight-based and circuit-based information improves robustness and handles polysemanticity through clustering.
Interpretability of features varies with layer depth, with early and late layers being more interpretable than middle layers.
Faithfulness scores are low across methods, suggesting individual feature interventions may not strongly affect outputs due to model redundancy.
papers.limitation:
Faithfulness is low across layers and methods, likely due to model redundancy; evaluating interventions on groups of features or entire circuits might be more trustworthy.
The validation step in WeightLens does not always succeed, as some weight-based connections are meaningful only in context and cannot be validated with single-token forward passes.
future_direction: Modifying the faithfulness metric to evaluate interventions on groups of features or entire circuits.
Exploring evaluation-guided refinement of clustering parameters and results in CircuitLens.
papers.abstract: The fields of explainable AI and mechanistic interpretability aim to uncover the internal structure of neural networks, with circuit discovery as a central tool for understanding model computations. Existing approaches, however, rely on manual inspection and remain limited to toy tasks. Automated interpretability offers scalability by analyzing isolated features and their activations, but it often misses interactions between features and depends strongly on external LLMs and dataset quality. Transcoders have recently made it possible to separate feature attributions into input-dependent and input-invariant components, providing a foundation for more systematic circuit analysis. Building on this, we propose WeightLens and CircuitLens, two complementary methods that go beyond activation-based analysis. WeightLens interprets features directly from their learned weights, removing the need for explainer models or datasets while matching or exceeding the performance of existing methods on context-independent features. CircuitLens captures how feature activations arise from interactions between components, revealing circuit-level dynamics that activation-only approaches cannot identify. Together, these methods increase interpretability robustness and enhance scalable mechanistic analysis of circuits while maintaining efficiency and quality.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: Analyzing Vision Transformers for Image Classification in Class Embedding Space
papers.research_question: How do Vision Transformers build categorical representations for image classification, and how do self-attention and MLP layers contribute to this process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework to project Vision Transformers' internal representations onto the class embedding space, enabling analysis of how class representations are built and the differential roles of self-attention and MLP layers via key-value memory pair mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework is a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability and explainability of Vision Transformers, providing insights into their category-building processes.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens develop class-specific representations from early stages, with class identifiability increasing across blocks.
Attention mechanisms and contextual information are crucial for building class representations; image tokens cannot develop class-identifiable representations in isolation.
Self-attention and MLP layers differentially contribute: MLP layers promote strong categorical updates in late blocks, while self-attention layers promote weaker but more disseminated updates earlier.
The framework can identify image regions important for class detection and outperforms linear probing in revealing task-relevant features.
Key-value memory pair mechanisms in MLP and self-attention layers are involved in building class representations, with agreement rates correlating with model accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Only studies Vision Transformers trained for image classification.
Does not explore model editing or performance improvement applications.
future_direction: Adapt the framework to models with other types of output embeddings.
Use the mechanistic insights for model editing or performance improvement.
papers.abstract: Despite the growing use of transformer models in computer vision, a mechanistic understanding of these networks is still needed. This work introduces a method to reverse-engineer Vision Transformers trained to solve image classification tasks. Inspired by previous research in NLP, we demonstrate how the inner representations at any level of the hierarchy can be projected onto the learned class embedding space to uncover how these networks build categorical representations for their predictions. We use our framework to show how image tokens develop class-specific representations that depend on attention mechanisms and contextual information, and give insights on how self-attention and MLP layers differentially contribute to this categorical composition. We additionally demonstrate that this method (1) can be used to determine the parts of an image that would be important for detecting the class of interest, and (2) exhibits significant advantages over traditional linear probing approaches. Taken together, our results position our proposed framework as a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability and explainability research.

papers.title: Learning Transformer Programs
papers.research_question: How can we train Transformers that are mechanistically interpretable by design, rather than reverse-engineering black-box models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for training Transformers that are interpretable by design, which can be automatically converted into discrete, human-readable programs after training.
papers.conclusion: Transformer Programs represent a promising step towards building intrinsically interpretable machine learning models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer Programs can achieve reasonable performance on a variety of tasks, including algorithmic problems and NLP tasks, comparable to standard Transformers of similar size.
The learned programs are easy to interpret and can be analyzed using standard code analysis tools, such as debuggers, to understand model behavior and debug errors.
The method faces optimization challenges, especially when scaling to larger vocabularies and sequence lengths, and the learned programs can be non-intuitive.
papers.limitation:
Optimization challenges make it difficult to scale to larger vocabularies and sequence lengths.
The learned programs can be complicated and non-intuitive, differing from human-written solutions.
future_direction: Scaling Transformer Programs to larger models and more complex tasks.
Developing methods for automatically analyzing the resulting programs and imposing inductive biases for more interpretable programs.
papers.abstract: Recent research in mechanistic interpretability has attempted to reverse-engineer Transformer models by carefully inspecting network weights and activations. However, these approaches require considerable manual effort and still fall short of providing complete, faithful descriptions of the underlying algorithms. In this work, we introduce a procedure for training Transformers that are mechanistically interpretable by design. We build on RASP [Weiss et al., 2021], a programming language that can be compiled into Transformer weights. Instead of compiling human-written programs into Transformers, we design a modified Transformer that can be trained using gradient-based optimization and then automatically converted into a discrete, human-readable program. We refer to these models as Transformer Programs. To validate our approach, we learn Transformer Programs for a variety of problems, including an in-context learning task, a suite of algorithmic problems (e.g. sorting, recognizing Dyck languages), and NLP tasks including named entity recognition and text classification. The Transformer Programs can automatically find reasonable solutions, performing on par with standard Transformers of comparable size; and, more importantly, they are easy to interpret. To demonstrate these advantages, we convert Transformers into Python programs and use off-the-shelf code analysis tools to debug model errors and identify the "circuits" used to solve different sub-problems. We hope that Transformer Programs open a new path toward the goal of intrinsically interpretable machine learning.

papers.title: Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Under what conditions does a transparent algorithm constitute a faithful interpretation of the known, but opaque, low-level details of a black box model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper generalizes the theory of causal abstraction from mechanism replacement to arbitrary mechanism transformation, and uses this framework to provide a flexible, precise formalization for core mechanistic interpretability concepts (polysemantic neurons, linear representation hypothesis, modular features, graded faithfulness) and to unify a wide range of existing interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Causal abstraction provides a solid theoretical foundation for mechanistic interpretability, enabling precise definitions of core concepts and a unified perspective on existing methods, which facilitates rigorous falsification through experimentation.
papers.key_findings:
Causal abstraction theory is generalized to allow for arbitrary mechanism transformations (interventionals), which enables the isolation of quantities distributed across overlapping sets of microvariables.
The core concepts of polysemantic neurons, the linear representation hypothesis, modular features, and graded faithfulness are given flexible, mathematically precise definitions within the causal abstraction framework.
A wide range of mechanistic interpretability methods (e.g., activation patching, causal scrubbing, sparse autoencoders, steering) and behavioral interpretability methods (e.g., LIME, integrated gradients) are unified under the common language of causal abstraction.
papers.abstract: Causal abstraction provides a theoretical foundation for mechanistic interpretability, the field concerned with providing intelligible algorithms that are faithful simplifications of the known, but opaque low-level details of black box AI models. Our contributions are (1) generalizing the theory of causal abstraction from mechanism replacement (i.e., hard and soft interventions) to arbitrary mechanism transformation (i.e., functionals from old mechanisms to new mechanisms), (2) providing a flexible, yet precise formalization for the core concepts of polysemantic neurons, the linear representation hypothesis, modular features, and graded faithfulness, and (3) unifying a variety of mechanistic interpretability methods in the common language of causal abstraction, namely, activation and path patching, causal mediation analysis, causal scrubbing, causal tracing, circuit analysis, concept erasure, sparse autoencoders, differential binary masking, distributed alignment search, and steering.

papers.title: Transformers trained on proteins can learn to attend to Euclidean distance
papers.research_question: How can standard Transformers learn to measure Euclidean distance and function as structure models for 3D data, such as proteins?
papers.core_contribution: Standard Transformers can learn to measure Euclidean distance and function as structure models when given linear embeddings of coordinates, without requiring architectural modifications.
papers.conclusion: Standard Transformers are capable of structural reasoning by learning SE(3)-invariant distance filters, providing a basis for using them as hybrid structure-language models for proteins and other 3D tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can learn to approximate a 3D Gaussian attention filter of relative distance when given linear embeddings of coordinates.
Transformers need at least n+2 embedding dimensions to learn distance in R^n.
Data augmentation with random rotations improves SE(3)-invariance and reduces overfitting.
Adding coordinates to a protein Transformer improves masked token prediction and sequence recovery, especially for amino acids with distinct backbone conformations.
Pretraining a protein Transformer with coordinates and then finetuning for function prediction outperforms custom structural models like DeepFRI.
future_direction: Applying the method to other domains like small molecules, 3D objects, vision Transformers, and large language models.
papers.abstract: While conventional Transformers generally operate on sequence data, they can be used in conjunction with structure models, typically SE(3)-invariant or equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs), for 3D applications such as protein structure modelling. These hybrids typically involve either (1) preprocessing/tokenizing structural features as input for Transformers or (2) taking Transformer embeddings and processing them within a structural representation. However, there is evidence that Transformers can learn to process structural information on their own, such as the AlphaFold3 structural diffusion model. In this work we show that Transformers can function independently as structure models when passed linear embeddings of coordinates. We first provide a theoretical explanation for how Transformers can learn to filter attention as a 3D Gaussian with learned variance. We then validate this theory using both simulated 3D points and in the context of masked token prediction for proteins. Finally, we show that pre-training protein Transformer encoders with structure improves performance on a downstream task, yielding better performance than custom structural models. Together, this work provides a basis for using standard Transformers as hybrid structure-language models.

papers.title: Explaining the Explainer: Understanding the Inner Workings of Transformer-based Symbolic Regression Models
papers.research_question: How can we understand the internal mechanisms of transformer-based symbolic regression models, specifically by identifying circuits responsible for generating symbolic operators?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PATCHES, a novel evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm for symbolic regression transformers, and establishes a formal evaluation framework (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) for circuit correctness.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes symbolic regression as a promising domain for mechanistic interpretability and provides a principled methodology for circuit discovery in such models.
papers.key_findings:
PATCHES successfully isolates circuits for specific symbolic operators (e.g., sin, add, log) in a transformer-based SR model.
Mean patching combined with functional evaluation (accuracy) is more reliable for discovering correct circuits than resample patching or model-based (logit) evaluation.
Direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features, limiting their utility for causal circuit discovery.
Circuits for SR are dense (40-78% of model components), attributed to the small vocabulary and complex syntactic encoding required.
papers.limitation:
Resample patching sometimes fails to sufficiently suppress the target token's information, hindering causal isolation and circuit discovery.
High baseline performance for some operators (e.g., addition) makes it difficult to achieve completeness, as patching does not degrade performance enough.
papers.abstract: Following their success across many domains, transformers have also proven effective for symbolic regression (SR); however, the internal mechanisms underlying their generation of mathematical operators remain largely unexplored. Although mechanistic interpretability has successfully identified circuits in language and vision models, it has not yet been applied to SR.
