papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability is a promising approach for achieving holistic explanations of AI systems and should be integrated into XAI research to meet important societal desiderata.
papers.key_findings:
Current XAI methods, while useful in specific contexts, fail to provide holistic explanations of how AI systems work as a whole.
Mechanistic interpretability, which applies discovery strategies from the life sciences, can reveal the functional organization of AI systems.
The case of Distill demonstrates that MI can successfully identify circuits (like curve detectors) and explain model behavior.
MI enables better prediction and control of AI systems, contributing to safety and trust.
MI is complementary to traditional XAI and should be accommodated in XAI research.
papers.limitation:
The complexity of large models makes mechanistic interpretability hopeless.
MI may be too resource-intensive.
MI may be unnecessary for many applications.
MI may be prone to overfitting and cherry-picking.
MI may be limited by the entanglement of representations in neural networks.
MI may be limited by the fact that neural networks are not modular.
papers.abstract: Abstract Recent work in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) attempts to render opaque AI systems understandable through a divide-and-conquer strategy. However, this fails to illuminate how trained AI systems work as a whole . Precisely this kind of functional understanding is needed, though, to satisfy important societal desiderata such as safety. To remedy this situation, we argue, AI researchers should seek mechanistic interpretability , viz. apply coordinated discovery strategies familiar from the life sciences to uncover the functional organisation of complex AI systems. Additionally, theorists should accommodate for the unique costs and benefits of such strategies in their portrayals of XAI research.

papers.title: Position-aware Automatic Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate positional information into automatic circuit discovery for language models to address limitations of position-agnostic methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces position-aware circuit discovery (PEAP) and dataset schemas to enable fully automated discovery of position-sensitive circuits, achieving better faithfulness than position-agnostic methods.
papers.conclusion: Position-aware circuit discovery and schemas improve circuit faithfulness and enable automated analysis of variable-length inputs, providing a more precise foundation for mechanistic explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Position-aware circuits are smaller and more faithful than position-agnostic circuits.
Automatically generated schemas (with or without saliency masks) yield circuits comparable to those from human-designed schemas.
The proposed method handles variable-length inputs via schemas, enabling circuit discovery in more naturalistic settings.
papers.limitation:
Schemas assume sequential order of spans, which may not hold for all datasets.
The schema generation and application pipeline may not always produce valid schemas for all examples.
future_direction: Relax the sequential order assumption in schemas to support greater variation across examples.
Investigate the components in the circuit for the Winobias task to understand the balance between task-relevant and bias-inducing factors.

papers.title: ACES-GNN: can graph neural network learn to explain activity cliffs?
papers.research_question: Can Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) be trained to provide better explanations for activity cliffs (structurally similar molecules with significant potency differences) while also improving prediction accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the ACES-GNN framework, which integrates explanation supervision for activity cliffs into GNN training, improving both predictive accuracy and the interpretability of molecular structure-property relationships.
papers.conclusion: ACES-GNN represents a promising direction for improving both the predictivity and interpretability of GNN models in QSAR applications, with the potential to accelerate lead optimization in drug discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ACES-GNN improves explainability (global direction) on 28 out of 30 datasets compared to unsupervised GNNs.
ACES-GNN improves prediction accuracy for activity cliff molecules, reducing RMSE_cliff.
A positive correlation exists between the improvement in prediction accuracy and the improvement in explanation quality.
The ACES framework is effective across different GNN backbones (MPNN, GIN, GAT).
Explanation supervision helps the model focus on uncommon substructures critical for activity cliffs, aligning attributions with chemist-friendly interpretations.
papers.limitation:
The ground-truth coloring relies on a fixed definition for activity cliff molecules, and some uncommon substructures between pairs may not be causative for potency changes.
The current GNN backbone does not outperform the Random Forest + ECFP combination in predictive accuracy or attribution quality across all datasets.
The validation process prioritizes minimizing RMSE during training rather than optimizing the explainability metric, so not all attributions after supervision achieve higher global direction accuracy.
future_direction: Incorporate geometric information into GNNs for further improvement.
Explore alternative gradient-based explanation techniques, such as expected gradients, to reduce potential biases.
Develop methods to identify true causal substructures in activity cliffs, enhancing explanation evaluation and guidance.
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have revolutionized molecular property prediction by leveraging graph-based representations, yet their opaque decision-making processes hinder broader adoption in drug discovery. This study introduces the Activity-Cliff-Explanation-Supervised GNN (ACES-GNN) framework, designed to simultaneously improve predictive accuracy and interpretability by integrating explanation supervision for activity cliffs (ACs) into GNN training. ACs, defined by structurally similar molecules with significant potency differences, pose challenges for traditional models due to their reliance on shared structural features. By aligning model attributions with chemist-friendly interpretations, the ACES-GNN framework bridges the gap between prediction and explanation. Validated across 30 pharmacological targets, ACES-GNN consistently enhances both predictive accuracy and attribution quality for ACs compared to unsupervised GNNs. Our results demonstrate a positive correlation between improved predictions and accurate explanations, offering a robust and adaptable framework to better understand and interpret ACs. This work underscores the potential of explanation-guided learning to advance interpretable artificial intelligence in molecular modeling and drug discovery.

papers.title: Localized Definitions and Distributed Reasoning: A Proof-of-Concept Mechanistic Interpretability Study via Activation Patching
papers.research_question: How is knowledge representation localized in fine-tuned language models, and how does it vary with task complexity?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that factual knowledge is localized while associative knowledge is distributed in fine-tuned models, and introduces CLAP for causal layer attribution.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is localized while associative reasoning depends on distributed intermediate representations, highlighting task-dependent knowledge organization.
papers.key_findings:
Patching the first feedforward layer recovered 56% of correct preference for associative knowledge, indicating distributed representations.
Patching the final output layer completely restored accuracy (100% recovery) for definitional knowledge, indicating localized representation.
Minimal recovery from convolutional layer patching (13.6%) suggests low-level features contribute marginally to high-level reasoning.
Statistical analysis confirmed significant layer-specific effects (p<0.01).
Editing efficacy depends on task type, with factual knowledge more localized and associative knowledge depending on distributed representations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis focused exclusively on PubMed epilepsy-related abstracts, potentially limiting generalizability to broader knowledge tasks.
Activation patching may generate false positives due to indirect causal pathways.
Exclusive focus on GPT-2 leaves open questions about scalability to other architectures.
future_direction: Cross-domain comparisons to better understand task-dependent representation patterns.
Methodological integration to improve efficiency.
Extensions to multimodal models where knowledge distribution mechanisms may differ significantly.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the localization of knowledge representation in fine-tuned GPT-2 models using Causal Layer Attribution via Activation Patching (CLAP), a method that identifies critical neural layers responsible for correct answer generation. The model was fine-tuned on 9,958 PubMed abstracts (epilepsy: 20,595 mentions, EEG: 11,674 mentions, seizure: 13,921 mentions) using two configurations with validation loss monitoring for early stopping. CLAP involved (1) caching clean (correct answer) and corrupted (incorrect answer) activations, (2) computing logit difference to quantify model preference, and (3) patching corrupted activations with clean ones to assess recovery. Results revealed three findings: First, patching the first feedforward layer recovered 56% of correct preference, demonstrating that associative knowledge is distributed across multiple layers. Second, patching the final output layer completely restored accuracy (100% recovery), indicating that definitional knowledge is localised. The stronger clean logit difference for definitional questions further supports this localized representation. Third, minimal recovery from convolutional layer patching (13.6%) suggests low-level features contribute marginally to high-level reasoning. Statistical analysis confirmed significant layer-specific effects (p<0.01). These findings demonstrate that factual knowledge is more localized and associative knowledge depends on distributed representations. We also showed that editing efficacy depends on task type. Our findings not only reconcile conflicting observations about localization in model editing but also emphasize on using task-adaptive techniques for reliable, interpretable updates.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs Philosophy
papers.research_question: How can philosophy contribute to mechanistic interpretability? The paper investigates three open problems in MI and how philosophy can help.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that mechanistic interpretability needs philosophy to clarify its concepts, refine its methods, and assess the epistemic and ethical stakes of interpreting AI systems.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that philosophy is deeply relevant to mechanistic interpretability and invites deeper interdisciplinary collaboration that is technically informed and philosophically grounded.
papers.key_findings:
Philosophy can help in decomposing networks into interpretable parts by providing conceptual tools from mechanistic explanation and challenging the assumption of a single true decomposition.
Philosophy can clarify the concept of 'features' in AI systems by distinguishing between vehicles and content of representations, refining experimental approaches, and suggesting new lines of investigation.
Philosophy can help in detecting deceptive behavior by clarifying concepts like lying and deception, guiding the search for AI beliefs, and drawing ethical and normative boundaries.
future_direction: Deeper interdisciplinary collaboration between philosophy and mechanistic interpretability.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to explain how neural networks work by uncovering their underlying causal mechanisms. As the field grows in influence, it is increasingly important to examine not just models themselves, but the assumptions, concepts and explanatory strategies implicit in MI research. We argue that mechanistic interpretability needs philosophy: not as an afterthought, but as an ongoing partner in clarifying its concepts, refining its methods, and assessing the epistemic and ethical stakes of interpreting AI systems. Taking three open problems from the MI literature as examples, this position paper illustrates the value philosophy can add to MI research, and outlines a path toward deeper interdisciplinary dialogue.

papers.title: Tensor Product Decomposition Networks: Uncovering Representations of Structure Learned by Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode compositional symbolic structure in their vector representations, and do they use tensor product representations?
papers.core_contribution: TPDNs show that RNNs can learn structured representations similar to tensor product representations for artificial tasks, but for real-world NLP tasks, representations are less structured, approximated by bag-of-words, suggesting training tasks may not induce robust structural representations.
papers.conclusion: RNNs trained on structure-sensitive tasks learn representations well approximated by tensor-product representations, but sentence encoders for NLP tasks show less structure, approximated by bag-of-words.
papers.key_findings:
TPDNs can closely approximate RNN representations for digit sequence copying tasks, indicating structured encoding.
Linear RNNs use bidirectional role schemes, while tree RNNs use tree position roles for representation.
For natural language processing models like InferSent and Skip-thought, representations are well approximated by bag-of-words, showing limited structure.
The nature of learned representations is related to the RNN's structure and the training task.
Training tasks influence whether networks discover structured or unstructured representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce an analysis technique for understanding compositional structure present in the vector representations used by neural networks. The inner workings of neural networks are notoriously difficult to understand, and in particular it is far from clear how they manage to perform remarkably well on tasks that depend on compositional structure even though they use continuous vector representations with no obvious compositional structure. Using our analysis technique, we show that the representations of these models can be closely approximated by Tensor Product Representations, a type of interpretable structure that lends significant insight into the workings of these hard-to-interpret models.

papers.title: Sparse Reward Subsystem in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states analogous to the biological reward subsystem, and what are its properties?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states, consisting of value neurons that encode state value and dopamine neurons that encode reward prediction error, and shows their critical role in reasoning and their robustness across models and tasks.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a sparse reward subsystem analogous to the biological reward subsystem, which is consistent across tasks, layers, model scales, and architectures, and has potential applications.
papers.key_findings:
Value neurons exist in LLM hidden states and can predict the value of the current state using only a small fraction of neurons.
Ablating even 1% of value neurons severely impairs reasoning performance, while random ablation does not.
Value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, layers, and architectural designs.
Value neurons are transferable across different datasets and across models fine-tuned from the same base model.
Dopamine neurons exist and encode reward prediction error, with activation patterns correlating with positive and negative surprises.
papers.limitation: Dopamine neurons are demonstrated primarily through case studies rather than quantitative metrics.
future_direction: Further explore applications of the reward subsystem for detecting and guiding LLM generation and reasoning.
Develop quantitative metrics for measuring dopamine neurons.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify a sparse reward subsystem within the hidden states of Large Language Models (LLMs), drawing an analogy to the biological reward subsystem in the human brain. We demonstrate that this subsystem contains value neurons that represent the model's internal expectation of state value, and through intervention experiments, we establish the importance of these neurons for reasoning. Our experiments reveal that these value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, and architectures; furthermore, they exhibit significant transferability across different datasets and models fine-tuned from the same base model. By examining cases where value predictions and actual rewards diverge, we identify dopamine neurons within the reward subsystem which encode reward prediction errors (RPE). These neurons exhibit high activation when the reward is higher than expected and low activation when the reward is lower than expected.

papers.title: Understanding the Failure Modes of Transformers through the Lens of Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the failure modes of transformers, and how can they be understood through the lens of graph neural network theory?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical understanding of transformer failure modes (over-smoothing, over-squashing, under-reaching) through the lens of GNN theory, and interprets existing ad-hoc solutions (like pause tokens and differential transformer) within this framework.
papers.conclusion: Theoretical issues like over-smoothing and over-squashing limit transformer improvement, and existing solutions are often ad-hoc; GNN theory provides a grounded perspective to guide future research.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers suffer from over-smoothing (rank collapse) due to repeated information mixing, similar to GNNs.
The causal mask in decoder-only transformers creates a position bias, leading to attention sinks and over-squashing of later tokens (the runway problem).
Existing solutions like pause tokens and the differential transformer can be interpreted as mitigating over-smoothing and the runway problem.
GNN theory offers a unified framework to understand transformer failure modes and explain why certain intuitive fixes work.
papers.abstract: Transformers and more specifically decoder-only transformers dominate modern LLM architectures. While they have shown to work exceptionally well, they are not without issues, resulting in surprising failure modes and predictably asymmetric performance degradation. This article is a study of many of these observed failure modes of transformers through the lens of graph neural network (GNN) theory. We first make the case that much of deep learning, including transformers, is about learnable information mixing and propagation. This makes the study of model failure modes a study of bottlenecks in information propagation. This naturally leads to GNN theory, where there is already a rich literature on information propagation bottlenecks and theoretical failure modes of models. We then make the case that many issues faced by GNNs are also experienced by transformers. In addition, we analyze how the causal nature of decoder-only transformers create interesting geometric properties in information propagation, resulting in predictable and potentially devastating failure modes. Finally, we observe that existing solutions in transformer research tend to be ad-hoc and driven by intuition rather than grounded theoretical motivation. As such, we unify many such solutions under a more theoretical perspective, providing insight into why they work, what problem they are actually solving, and how they can be further improved to target specific failure modes of transformers. Overall, this article is an attempt to bridge the gap between observed failure modes in transformers and a general lack of theoretical understanding of them in this space.

papers.title: Modular addition without black-boxes: Compressing explanations of MLPs that compute numerical integration
papers.research_question: How can we compress nonlinear feature-maps (MLP layers) in neural networks to understand their internal algorithms? The paper presents a case study on modular addition models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a method to compress nonlinear feature-maps in MLP layers by interpreting them as performing numerical integration, demonstrated on modular addition models.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a first case study in rigorously compressing nonlinear feature-maps, demonstrating that interpreting feature-maps reveals additional insight about model mechanisms and hopes to inspire further study.
papers.key_findings:
The MLP in modular addition models can be interpreted as performing numerical integration to double the frequency of input representations.
Neurons have primary and secondary frequencies, with output phases approximately double the input phases.
Secondary frequencies compensate for weaknesses in the 'pizza' algorithm when |cos(k(a-b)/2)| is small.
Non-vacuous bounds on MLP outputs can be derived in time linear in the number of parameters.
The infinite-width lens allows turning post-activation matrix multiplications into approximate integrals for analysis.
papers.limitation: The error bounds derived are not tight because the understanding of numerical integration in the network is incomplete.
future_direction: Developing automated tools for approximating and interpreting neural networks using low-rank approximations like Fourier expansion.
Improving error bounds and parameterizations of the model to account for all components.
papers.abstract: The goal of mechanistic interpretability is discovering simpler, low-rank algorithms implemented by models. While we can compress activations into features, compressing nonlinear feature-maps -- like MLP layers -- is an open problem. In this work, we present the first case study in rigorously compressing nonlinear feature-maps, which are the leading asymptotic bottleneck to compressing small transformer models. We work in the classic setting of the modular addition models, and target a non-vacuous bound on the behaviour of the ReLU MLP in time linear in the parameter-count of the circuit. To study the ReLU MLP analytically, we use the infinite-width lens, which turns post-activation matrix multiplications into approximate integrals. We discover a novel interpretation of} the MLP layer in one-layer transformers implementing the ``pizza'' algorithm: the MLP can be understood as evaluating a quadrature scheme, where each neuron computes the area of a rectangle under the curve of a trigonometric integral identity. Our code is available at https://tinyurl.com/mod-add-integration.

papers.title: Decomposition of Small Transformer Models
papers.research_question: Can Stochastic Parameter Decomposition (SPD) be extended to Transformer models to decompose their weights into interpretable, causally relevant subcomponents?
papers.core_contribution: Extends Stochastic Parameter Decomposition (SPD) to Transformer models by proposing a causal importance function for sequential data and a new loss function, demonstrating that SPD can recover interpretable parameter-space mechanisms in both a toy induction-head model and GPT-2-small.
papers.conclusion: Parameter decomposition can surface semantically specific mechanisms in Transformers, and SPD yields narrow, causally relevant directions that act as clean handles for mechanistic interventions.
papers.key_findings:
SPD successfully decomposes a toy induction-head model and recovers the expected 2-step copy circuit.
Applying SPD to GPT-2-small locates subcomponents corresponding to interpretable concepts like 'golf' and 'basketball'.
Ablating the recovered rank-1 slices selectively reduces the probability of the targeted fact (e.g., 'golf' for Tiger Woods) while leaving unrelated examples largely unaffected.
The method achieves a 99% size reduction in active subcomponents for the GPT-2-small fact examples compared to the full model.
Facts like athlete-sport associations can originate as early as the first MLP layer and propagate through the network.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are restricted to small-scale models, leaving open questions about scalability to larger architectures.
The causal importance parameterisation introduces additional computational overhead.
Evaluation is qualitative and task-specific, so further benchmarks are needed to establish generality across architectures and tasks.
Difficulty in establishing ground truth even for small, toy Transformers.
future_direction: Extend this work to larger models.
Improve the definition of causal importance for computations with feature interactions.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that decomposing models in parameter space may yield clean handles for analysis and intervention. Previous methods have demonstrated successful applications on a wide range of toy models, but the gap to "real models" has not yet been bridged. In this work, we extend Stochastic Parameter Decomposition (SPD) to Transformer models, proposing an updated causal importance function suited for sequential data and a new loss function. We demonstrate that SPD can successfully decompose a toy induction-head model and recover the expected 2-step circuit. We also show that applying SPD to GPT-2-small can successfully locate subcomponents corresponding to interpretable concepts like "golf" and "basketball". These results take the first step in the direction of extending SPD to modern models, and show that we can use the method to surface interpretable parameter-space mechanisms.

papers.title: Transformers learn factored representations
papers.research_question: Do transformers learn to factor their world into parts from next-token prediction, and why would they have an inductive bias for factored representations?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers learn to factor their world into parts, representing each factor in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream, and show an inductive bias toward factored representations even when it is lossy.
papers.conclusion: Transformers decompose the world into parts and represent them in orthogonal subspaces due to an inductive bias from next-token prediction, suggesting interpretable low-dimensional structure may persist in models trained on complex data.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn factored representations in orthogonal subspaces when data has conditionally independent factors.
The dimensionality of activations collapses to the linearly growing factored prediction, not the exponentially growing joint representation.
Factor subspaces become approximately orthogonal over training, as measured by subspace overlap and dimensionality additivity.
Factoring begins at the token embedding layer, with the embedding matrix developing low-rank structure corresponding to factor subspaces.
Transformers exhibit an inductive bias toward factored representations, learning them early even when data is not perfectly factorable, sacrificing fidelity for dimensional efficiency.
papers.limitation: Experiments are conducted on synthetic data with known latent structure, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Investigate whether differences in factorization behavior between transformers, RNNs, and LSTMs are due to training dynamics or inductive bias.
papers.abstract: Transformers pretrained via next token prediction learn to factor their world into parts, representing these factors in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream. We formalize two representational hypotheses: (1) a representation in the product space of all factors, whose dimension grows exponentially with the number of parts, or (2) a factored representation in orthogonal subspaces, whose dimension grows linearly. The factored representation is lossless when factors are conditionally independent, but sacrifices predictive fidelity otherwise, creating a tradeoff between dimensional efficiency and accuracy. We derive precise predictions about the geometric structure of activations for each, including the number of subspaces, their dimensionality, and the arrangement of context embeddings within them. We test between these hypotheses on transformers trained on synthetic processes with known latent structure. Models learn factored representations when factors are conditionally independent, and continue to favor them early in training even when noise or hidden dependencies undermine conditional independence, reflecting an inductive bias toward factoring at the cost of fidelity. This provides a principled explanation for why transformers decompose the world into parts, and suggests that interpretable low dimensional structure may persist even in models trained on complex data.

papers.title: APP: Accelerated Path Patching with Task-Specific Pruning
papers.research_question: Can pruning be used for circuit discovery, and how can we accelerate path patching by reducing the search space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid method that uses Contrastive-FLAP pruning to reduce the search space for circuit discovery, achieving significant speedups while recovering minimal circuits with performance comparable to standard path patching.
papers.conclusion: APP provides a scalable preprocessing step for circuit discovery, making mechanistic interpretability more efficient and practical for large models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning alone cannot recover minimal circuits; circuits found by pruning are larger than those found by path patching.
Contrastive-FLAP, a novel pruning method, better preserves task-specific attention heads compared to vanilla FLAP.
APP reduces the search space for circuit discovery by an average of 56%, leading to speedups of 59.63%-93.27% compared to standard path patching.
Circuits discovered by APP have substantial overlap and similar performance to those found by standard path patching.
APP enables circuit discovery to scale to larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) by reducing computational costs.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter search is limited by computational cost, especially for large models.
Trade-off between circuit size and performance requires researcher discretion.
APP focuses on attention heads and does not include MLP components, which may be important for some tasks.
The true positive rate of hybrid FLAP caps the ability to recover all heads in the circuit.
future_direction: Extending APP to other circuit discovery algorithms like ACDC.
Incorporating MLP components into the automated path patching method.
Studying whether circuits discovered in GPT-2 small translate to larger models.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery is a key step in many mechanistic interpretability pipelines. Current methods, such as Path Patching, are computationally expensive and have limited in-depth circuit analysis for smaller models. In this study, we propose Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid approach leveraging our novel contrastive attention head pruning method to drastically reduce the search space of circuit discovery methods. Our Contrastive-FLAP pruning algorithm uses techniques from causal mediation analysis to assign higher pruning scores to task-specific attention heads, leading to higher performing sparse models compared to traditional pruning techniques. Although Contrastive-FLAP is successful at preserving task-specific heads that existing pruning algorithms remove at low sparsity ratios, the circuits found by Contrastive-FLAP alone are too large to satisfy the minimality constraint required in circuit analysis. APP first applies Contrastive-FLAP to reduce the search space on required for circuit discovery algorithms by, on average, 56\%. Next, APP, applies traditional Path Patching on the remaining attention heads, leading to a speed up of 59.63\%-93.27\% compared to Path Patching applied to the dense model. Despite the substantial computational saving that APP provides, circuits obtained from APP exhibit substantial overlap and similar performance to previously established Path Patching circuits

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Model Metamers Reveal Invariances in Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do the invariance properties of graph neural networks (GNNs) compare to human perceptual invariances, and can we quantify and mitigate excessive invariance in GNNs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a metamer generation technique for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to investigate their representational invariance, revealing excessive invariance in standard architectures and proposing architectural and training modifications to mitigate it.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a framework for generating model metamers in GNNs to uncover and quantify representational invariance, exposing a misalignment with human perception and providing tools for benchmarking and improving sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
Standard GNN architectures exhibit pronounced over-invariance, mapping structurally or semantically different graphs to nearly identical internal activations.
Architectural and training modifications (e.g., replacing ReLU with ELU, adversarial training, adding residual connections) can mitigate over-invariance.
Increasing the hidden layer dimension of a GNN reduces over-invariance by increasing the rank of the model's Jacobian.
Invariance increases with network depth, as feature metamers generated from deeper layers become less similar to the original input.
Cross-model invariance analysis reveals that invariances learned by GNNs comprise both shared components and architecture-specific features.
future_direction: Extend the approach to more graph tasks.
Apply the method to broader model families.
Develop improved metamer generation techniques.
papers.abstract: In recent years, deep neural networks have been extensively employed in perceptual systems to learn representations endowed with invariances, aiming to emulate the invariance mechanisms observed in the human brain. However, studies in the visual and auditory domains have confirmed that significant gaps remain between the invariance properties of artificial neural networks and those of humans. To investigate the invariance behavior within graph neural networks (GNNs), we introduce a model ``metamers'' generation technique. By optimizing input graphs such that their internal node activations match those of a reference graph, we obtain graphs that are equivalent in the model's representation space, yet differ significantly in both structure and node features. Our theoretical analysis focuses on two aspects: the local metamer dimension for a single node and the activation-induced volume change of the metamer manifold. Utilizing this approach, we uncover extreme levels of representational invariance across several classic GNN architectures. Although targeted modifications to model architecture and training strategies can partially mitigate this excessive invariance, they fail to fundamentally bridge the gap to human-like invariance. Finally, we quantify the deviation between metamer graphs and their original counterparts, revealing unique failure modes of current GNNs and providing a complementary benchmark for model evaluation.

papers.title: Symbolic Synthesis of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be combined with symbolic programs to improve data-efficient generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces G-SSNNs, a class of neural modules that inject features from synthesized symbolic programs to improve data efficiency and generalization.
papers.conclusion: G-SSNNs improve data efficiency and generalization on a binary prediction task over Raven's Progressive Matrices and allow derivation of symbolic program semantics without manual engineering.
papers.key_findings:
G-SSNN modules modulate the data efficiency and generalization of baseline neural models, creating predictable patterns of both heightened and curtailed generalization.
Training G-SSNNs provides information about desirable semantics of symbolic programs without manual engineering, which is compact and amenable to abstraction.
future_direction: Investigate data efficient generalization and the transferability of learned symbolic representations in more complex G-SSNN designs based on more complex classes of symbolic programs.
papers.abstract: Neural networks adapt very well to distributed and continuous representations, but struggle to generalize from small amounts of data. Symbolic systems commonly achieve data efficient generalization by exploiting modularity to benefit from local and discrete features of a representation. These features allow symbolic programs to be improved one module at a time and to experience combinatorial growth in the values they can successfully process. However, it is difficult to design a component that can be used to form symbolic abstractions and which is adequately overparametrized to learn arbitrary high-dimensional transformations. I present Graph-based Symbolically Synthesized Neural Networks (G-SSNNs), a class of neural modules that operate on representations modified with synthesized symbolic programs to include a fixed set of local and discrete features. I demonstrate that the choice of injected features within a G-SSNN module modulates the data efficiency and generalization of baseline neural models, creating predictable patterns of both heightened and curtailed generalization. By training G-SSNNs, we also derive information about desirable semantics of symbolic programs without manual engineering. This information is compact and amenable to abstraction, but can also be flexibly recontextualized for other high-dimensional settings. In future work, I will investigate data efficient generalization and the transferability of learned symbolic representations in more complex G-SSNN designs based on more complex classes of symbolic programs. Experimental code and data are available at https://github.com/shlomenu/symbolically_synthesized_networks .

papers.title: Transformer Circuit Faithfulness Metrics are not Robust
papers.research_question: What do circuit faithfulness metrics actually show? To what extent are they a useful test of the circuit and to what extent are they a reflection of the experimental methodology?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit faithfulness metrics are highly sensitive to seemingly minor variations in ablation methodology, meaning the optimal circuit for a task depends on the evaluation method used.
papers.conclusion: Existing circuit faithfulness metrics are not robust and reflect methodological choices as much as the circuit itself, necessitating clearer claims about circuits in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Faithfulness scores vary significantly between node-level and edge-level ablation.
Faithfulness scores vary between using mean ablation and resample ablation.
Whether token positions are distinguished during ablation affects faithfulness scores.
The order of computing averages (average of logit differences vs. average of percentages) changes the reported faithfulness.
There is high variance in faithfulness scores across individual prompts within a task distribution.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability work attempts to reverse engineer the learned algorithms present inside neural networks. One focus of this work has been to discover 'circuits' -- subgraphs of the full model that explain behaviour on specific tasks. But how do we measure the performance of such circuits? Prior work has attempted to measure circuit 'faithfulness' -- the degree to which the circuit replicates the performance of the full model. In this work, we survey many considerations for designing experiments that measure circuit faithfulness by ablating portions of the model's computation. Concerningly, we find existing methods are highly sensitive to seemingly insignificant changes in the ablation methodology. We conclude that existing circuit faithfulness scores reflect both the methodological choices of researchers as well as the actual components of the circuit - the task a circuit is required to perform depends on the ablation used to test it. The ultimate goal of mechanistic interpretability work is to understand neural networks, so we emphasize the need for more clarity in the precise claims being made about circuits. We open source a library at https://github.com/UFO-101/auto-circuit that includes highly efficient implementations of a wide range of ablation methodologies and circuit discovery algorithms.

papers.title: Mechanistic Data Attribution: Tracing the Training Origins of Interpretable LLM Units
papers.research_question: How can we trace the training data origins of interpretable circuits in LLMs, and what causal role do specific training samples play in the formation of these circuits?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Mechanistic Data Attribution (MDA) framework to trace training data origins of interpretable units in LLMs, and provides causal evidence linking induction heads to in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The MDA framework enables tracing training data origins of interpretable units and provides causal insights into circuit formation, with practical applications for data augmentation and model steering.
papers.key_findings:
Targeted intervention (removing or augmenting high-influence samples) significantly modulates the emergence of interpretable heads, while random interventions show no effect.
Repetitive structural data (e.g., LaTeX, XML) acts as a mechanistic catalyst for induction head formation.
High-influence samples are transferable across different induction heads, indicating mechanism-specific drivers.
Induction head formation follows a steady accumulation model, with high-influence samples primarily modulating the rate of emergence.
Interventions targeting induction head formation induce concurrent changes in the model's in-context learning capability, providing causal evidence for their functional link.
papers.limitation: The computational cost of the MDA framework is prohibitive for dense influence analysis over the entire training lifecycle.
future_direction: Investigating the complex multi-head dynamics and circuit reconfiguration in larger models.
papers.abstract: While Mechanistic Interpretability has identified interpretable circuits in LLMs, their causal origins in training data remain elusive. We introduce Mechanistic Data Attribution (MDA), a scalable framework that employs Influence Functions to trace interpretable units back to specific training samples. Through extensive experiments on the Pythia family, we causally validate that targeted intervention--removing or augmenting a small fraction of high-influence samples--significantly modulates the emergence of interpretable heads, whereas random interventions show no effect. Our analysis reveals that repetitive structural data (e.g., LaTeX, XML) acts as a mechanistic catalyst. Furthermore, we observe that interventions targeting induction head formation induce a concurrent change in the model's in-context learning (ICL) capability. This provides direct causal evidence for the long-standing hypothesis regarding the functional link between induction heads and ICL. Finally, we propose a mechanistic data augmentation pipeline that consistently accelerates circuit convergence across model scales, providing a principled methodology for steering the developmental trajectories of LLMs.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: Disentangling Polysemantic Channels in Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic channels in convolutional neural networks be identified and disentangled into monosemantic channels to improve interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an algorithm to identify and disentangle polysemantic channels in pre-trained CNNs into multiple channels, each activating for a single concept, without affecting predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: The introduced tool effectively identifies and disentangles γ-polysemantic channels in CNNs, enhancing mechanistic interpretability and feature visualization.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully disentangles polysemantic channels, as shown with channel #1660 for 'digital clock' and 'cauliflower' concepts, where disentangled channels mimic original activations for their respective concepts.
Quantitative analysis shows that for polysemantic channels, the first disentangled channel activates strongly for concept 1 (114% relative activation) and weakly for concept 2 (-9%), while the second shows the opposite pattern.
The residual channel has near-zero activation, indicating it captures minimal information beyond the disentangled concepts.
Feature visualizations (e.g., with MACO) for disentangled channels show more isolated concepts compared to the original polysemantic channel.
The approach is based on attribution methods and cosine similarity of average relevance vectors to identify polysemanticity.
papers.limitation:
Currently only applied to disentanglement of two concepts.
The formulation of polysemanticity is based on class labels, which may work better in later layers with more semantically meaningful concepts.
Relies on handpicked hyperparameters (τ, γ, p) for identification, which are application-specific.
future_direction: Extend the method to more than two concepts, e.g., through recursive application.
Explore the impact of hyperparameters and develop methods for setting them automatically.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability is concerned with analyzing individual components in a (convolutional) neural network (CNN) and how they form larger circuits representing decision mechanisms. These investigations are challenging since CNNs frequently learn polysemantic channels that encode distinct concepts, making them hard to interpret. To address this, we propose an algorithm to disentangle a specific kind of polysemantic channel into multiple channels, each responding to a single concept. Our approach restructures weights in a CNN, utilizing that different concepts within the same channel exhibit distinct activation patterns in the previous layer. By disentangling these polysemantic features, we enhance the interpretability of CNNs, ultimately improving explanatory techniques such as feature visualizations.

papers.title: LLaVA Steering: Visual Instruction Tuning with 500x Fewer Parameters through Modality Linear Representation-Steering
papers.research_question: How can the number of trainable parameters for visual instruction tuning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be significantly reduced by addressing the intrinsic imbalance between text and visual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Modality Linear Representation-Steering (MoReS), a method that rebalances text and visual modalities in MLLMs by steering visual representations through linear transformations, achieving comparable performance to LoRA with 500x fewer trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: MoReS provides an efficient and effective approach for visual instruction tuning in MLLMs by addressing modality imbalance, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offering a pathway for more accessible and customizable multimodal model development.
papers.key_findings:
MoReS requires 287 to 1,150 times fewer trainable parameters than LoRA while maintaining competitive performance on multiple visual benchmarks.
MoReS effectively rebalances the attention distribution between visual and textual representations, mitigating the intrinsic modality imbalance in MLLMs.
The method reduces hallucination in MLLMs, as shown by improved performance on POPE and HallucinationBench.
MoReS preserves the LLM's pre-trained world knowledge and performs well on text-only tasks, demonstrating its generalizability.
A dynamic steering ratio mechanism allows MoReS to adapt to tasks of varying complexity, with optimal ratios differing per dataset.
papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Activation Control for Efficiently Eliciting Long Chain-of-thought Ability of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning ability in large language models be efficiently elicited by understanding and controlling internal activation mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a training-free activation control method (EELo-CoT) that elicits long chain-of-thought reasoning by amplifying key MLP activations and inserting 'wait' tokens, and a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a small amplification module and LoRA layers.
papers.conclusion: By identifying and controlling a small set of key activations, the long chain-of-thought ability can be efficiently elicited in LLMs, leading to improved reasoning performance and self-reflection.
papers.key_findings:
Long-CoT related activations are sparse and primarily located in the last few layers of the model.
Amplifying these key activations and inserting 'wait' tokens can induce long CoT reasoning, increasing self-reflection rate and accuracy.
Activation changes around trigger tokens follow predictable patterns (sharp rise then logarithmic decay).
The proposed training-free EELo-CoT method improves accuracy and self-reflection on math and science reasoning benchmarks.
A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, training only 1.51% of parameters, outperforms LoRA and matches full fine-tuning on some benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
The activation intervention rules are simple and may not capture nuanced activation patterns that require more sophisticated stimulation.
Experiments are limited to models up to 32B parameters and do not extend to ultra-large or mixture-of-experts architectures.
The focus on self-reflection does not disentangle other latent capabilities that may be triggered by long CoT, such as elaboration without verification or memorization.
future_direction: Apply the method to multimodal LLMs (e.g., VLM and Video-LLM).
Test the method on more complex planning tasks (e.g., visual reasoning and GUI operation).
Test the generalizability of the method to non-transformer architectures (e.g., Mamba).
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable reasoning performance, eliciting the long chain-of-thought (CoT) ability in large language models (LLMs) typically requires costly reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning on high-quality distilled data. We investigate the internal mechanisms behind this capability and show that a small set of high-impact activations in the last few layers largely governs long-form reasoning attributes, such as output length and self-reflection. By simply amplifying these activations and inserting "wait" tokens, we can invoke the long CoT ability without any training, resulting in significantly increased self-reflection rates and accuracy. Moreover, we find that the activation dynamics follow predictable trajectories, with a sharp rise after special tokens and a subsequent exponential decay. Building on these insights, we introduce a general training-free activation control technique. It leverages a few contrastive examples to identify key activations, and employs simple analytic functions to modulate their values at inference time to elicit long CoTs. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of our method in efficiently eliciting long CoT reasoning in LLMs and improving their performance. Additionally, we propose a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a last-layer activation amplification module and a few LoRA layers, outperforming full LoRA fine-tuning on reasoning benchmarks with significantly fewer parameters. Our code and data are publicly released.

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: Everything, Everywhere, All at Once: Is Mechanistic Interpretability Identifiable?
papers.research_question: For a fixed behavior to explain, under the criteria that mechanistic interpretability sets for itself, are we guaranteed a unique explanation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that under current mechanistic interpretability criteria, explanations are not identifiable: multiple incompatible circuits and interpretations can satisfy the criteria for a given model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The lack of identifiability challenges the intuition that a unique explanation exists; the paper discusses pragmatic stances and suggests stricter criteria if unicity is desired.
papers.key_findings:
Multiple circuits can perfectly replicate the model's behavior (zero circuit error).
For a given circuit, multiple valid interpretations exist.
Several algorithms can be perfectly causally aligned with the neural computation (IIA of one).
For a given causally aligned algorithm, multiple subspaces of the neural network can be equally aligned.
The number of computational abstractions increases with network size and decreases with the number of training tasks.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are conducted in controlled, small-scale settings with simple tasks and small MLPs.
The reported number of circuits is a lower bound due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Introducing additional heuristics such as sparsity to resolve identifiability.
Using causal abstraction to require that all lower-level states are accounted for.
Adopting the inner interpretability framework that requires validation by multiple complementary criteria.
papers.abstract: As AI systems are used in high-stakes applications, ensuring interpretability is crucial. Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aims to reverse-engineer neural networks by extracting human-understandable algorithms to explain their behavior. This work examines a key question: for a given behavior, and under MI's criteria, does a unique explanation exist? Drawing on identifiability in statistics, where parameters are uniquely inferred under specific assumptions, we explore the identifiability of MI explanations. We identify two main MI strategies: (1) "where-then-what," which isolates a circuit replicating model behavior before interpreting it, and (2) "what-then-where," which starts with candidate algorithms and searches for neural activation subspaces implementing them, using causal alignment. We test both strategies on Boolean functions and small multi-layer perceptrons, fully enumerating candidate explanations. Our experiments reveal systematic non-identifiability: multiple circuits can replicate behavior, a circuit can have multiple interpretations, several algorithms can align with the network, and one algorithm can align with different subspaces. Is uniqueness necessary? A pragmatic approach may require only predictive and manipulability standards. If uniqueness is essential for understanding, stricter criteria may be needed. We also reference the inner interpretability framework, which validates explanations through multiple criteria. This work contributes to defining explanation standards in AI.

papers.title: Multimodal Task Vectors Enable Many-Shot Multimodal In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How to enable Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) to perform many-shot in-context learning without being limited by context length, by compressing examples into implicit representations (task vectors) in the model's attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Multimodal Task Vectors (MTV), compact implicit representations of in-context examples stored in attention heads, enabling many-shot multimodal in-context learning without fine-tuning and overcoming context length limitations.
papers.conclusion: MTV enables many-shot multimodal in-context learning, scales with examples, and generalizes to similar tasks without requiring fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
MTV outperforms zero-shot and few-shot ICL on various vision-language tasks.
MTV performance scales with the number of compressed examples (shots and iterations).
MTV can be used alongside explicit few-shot examples, freeing up context length.
MTV attention heads extracted on one task can generalize to similar out-of-domain tasks.
papers.limitation:
MTV requires interleaved LMMs and may not work as well on non-interleaved models.
Computing mean activations requires multiple forward passes, which can be computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: The recent success of interleaved Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) in few-shot learning suggests that in-context learning (ICL) with many examples can be promising for learning new tasks. However, this many-shot multimodal ICL setting has one crucial problem: it is fundamentally limited by the model's context length set at pretraining. The problem is especially prominent in the multimodal domain, which processes both text and images, requiring additional tokens. This motivates the need for a multimodal method to compress many shots into fewer tokens without finetuning. In this work, we enable LMMs to perform multimodal, many-shot in-context learning by leveraging Multimodal Task Vectors (MTV) -- compact implicit representations of in-context examples compressed in the model's attention heads. Specifically, we first demonstrate the existence of such MTV in LMMs and then leverage these extracted MTV to enable many-shot in-context learning for various vision-and-language tasks. Our experiments suggest that MTV can scale in performance with the number of compressed shots and generalize to similar out-of-domain tasks without additional context length for inference. Code: https://github.com/Brandon3964/MultiModal-Task-Vector

papers.title: Investigating the Reliability and Interpretability of Machine Learning Frameworks for Chemical Retrosynthesis
papers.abstract: Machine learning models for chemical retrosynthesis have attracted substantial interest in recent years. Unaddressed challenges, particularly the absence of robust evaluation metrics for performance comparison, and the lack of black-box interpretability, obscure model limitations and impede progress in the field. We present an automated benchmarking pipeline designed for effective model performance comparisons. With an emphasis on user-friendly design, we aim to streamline accessibility and facilitate utilisation within the research community. Additionally, we suggest and perform a new interpretability study to uncover the degree of chemical understanding acquired by retrosynthesis models. Our results reveal that frameworks based on chemical reaction rules yield the most diverse, chemically valid, and feasible reactions, whereas purely data-driven frameworks suffer from unfeasible and invalid predictions. The interpretability study emphasises that incorporating reaction rules not only enhances model performance but also improves interpretability. For simple molecules, we demonstrate that Graph Neural Networks identify relevant functional groups within the product molecule, providing thermodynamic stabilisation over the reactant precursors. In contrast, the popular Transformer fails to identify such crucial stabilisation. As the molecule and reaction mechanism grow more complex, both data-driven models propose unfeasible disconnections without offering a chemical rationale. We stress the importance of incorporating chemically meaningful descriptors within deep-learning models. Our study provides valuable guidance for the future development of retrosynthesis frameworks.

papers.title: A Unified View of Deep Learning for Reaction and Retrosynthesis Prediction: Current Status and Future Challenges
papers.abstract: Reaction and retrosynthesis prediction are fundamental tasks in computational chemistry that have recently garnered attention from both the machine learning and drug discovery communities. Various deep learning approaches have been proposed to tackle these problems, and some have achieved initial success. In this survey, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of advanced deep learning-based models for reaction and retrosynthesis prediction. We summarize the design mechanisms, strengths, and weaknesses of state-of-the-art approaches. Then, we discuss the limitations of current solutions and open challenges in the problem itself. Finally, we present promising directions to facilitate future research. To our knowledge, this paper is the first comprehensive and systematic survey that seeks to provide a unified understanding of reaction and retrosynthesis prediction.

papers.title: Retro-MTGR: Molecule Retrosynthesis Prediction via Multi-Task Graph Representation Learning
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> It is a vital bridging step to infer appropriate synthesis reaction routes (i.e., retrosynthesis) of newly-designed molecules. Unlike classical experience-based retrosynthesis approaches, artificial intelligence enables a cheap and fast retrosynthesis approach. Template-based models, limited in known synthesis templates, leverage substructure searching to infer candidate reaction centers (i.e., bonds). In contrast, both translation-based models (TransMs) and discriminative methods (DiscMs) are free to synthesis templates. TransM regards retrosynthesis as a translation from the target molecule to its reactants by generative algorithms. DiscM, directly inspired by chemical synthesis, performs reaction center recognition and leaving group identification in turn. Nevertheless, TransMs are redundant and weakly interpretable, while existing DiscMs neglect the associations between reaction centers and leaving groups. To address these issues, this paper elaborates a novel discriminative Multi-Task Graph Representation learning model of Retrosynthesis prediction (Retro-MTGR). It solves two major supervised discriminative tasks (i.e., the reaction center recognition and the leaving group identification respectively), and an auxiliary self-supervised task (i.e., atom embedding enhancer) simultaneously. The comparison with various state-of-the-art methods first demonstrates the superiority of Retro-MTGR. Then, the ablation studies reveal how its crucial components contribute to the prediction respectively, including the atom embedding enhancer, bond energies, and the leaving group co-occurrence graph. More importantly, comprehensive investigations validate its chemical interpretability by answering two questions: why a bond can be the reaction center or not, and what leaving groups are appropriate to given synthons. The answers demonstrate that Retro-MTGR can reflect five underlying chemical synthesis rules by characterizing molecule structures alone. Finally, two case studies demonstrate that the inferred retrosynthesis routes by Retro-MTGR are significantly consistent with those achieved by performed chemical synthesis assays. It’s anticipated that our Retro-MTGR can provide prior guidance for real retrosynthesis route planning. The code and data underlying this article are freely available at https://github.com/zpczaizheli/Retro-MTGR.

papers.title: Hierarchical Framework for Retrosynthesis Prediction with Enhanced Reaction Center Localization
papers.abstract: Retrosynthesis is essential for designing synthetic pathways for complex molecules and can be revolutionized by AI to automate and accelerate chemical synthesis planning for drug discovery and materials science. Here, we propose a hierarchical framework for retrosynthesis prediction that systematically integrates reaction center identification, action prediction, and termination decision into a unified pipeline. Leveraging a molecular encoder pretrained with contrastive learning, the model captures both atom and bond level representations, enabling accurate identification of reaction centers and prediction of chemical actions. The framework addresses the scarcity of multiple reaction center data through augmentation strategies, enhancing the ability of the model to generalize to diverse reaction scenarios. The proposed approach achieves competitive performance across benchmark datasets, with notably high topk accuracy and exceptional reaction center identification capabilities, demonstrating its robustness in handling complex transformations. These advancements position the framework as a promising tool for future applications in material design and drug discovery.

papers.title: Forward Reaction Prediction as Reverse Verification: A Novel Approach to Retrosynthesis
papers.abstract: Pupils' intuitive knowledge can lead them to verify multiplication by means of division. Based on this analogy, this study introduces the basic reverse verification concept to verify retrosynthesis through forward reaction. In this work, we present a "combined" model approach for retrosynthetic reaction prediction, where the first model is applied to retrosynthesis, and the second model, which is a "verified" model, is applied to the forward reaction prediction to verify the top-n reactants predicted by the retrosynthetic model. Using a "combined" model borrowed from human language translation, sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) + transformer models, we improve the top-1 accuracy of retrosynthetic prediction by 4.3% (37.4% vs 41.7%). The application of the similarity + seq2seq models increases the top-1 accuracy by 4.6% (52.9% vs 57.5%). In this way, we can not only improve the accuracy but also automate the evaluation of the synthetic route.

papers.title: MechRetro is a chemical-mechanism-driven graph learning framework for interpretable retrosynthesis prediction and pathway planning
papers.abstract: Leveraging artificial intelligence for automatic retrosynthesis speeds up organic pathway planning in digital laboratories. However, existing deep learning approaches are unexplainable, like "black box" with few insights, notably limiting their applications in real retrosynthesis scenarios. Here, we propose MechRetro, a chemical-mechanism-driven graph learning framework for interpretable retrosynthetic prediction and pathway planning, which learns several retrosynthetic actions to simulate a reverse reaction via elaborate self-adaptive joint learning. By integrating chemical knowledge as prior information, we design a novel Graph Transformer architecture to adaptively learn discriminative and chemically meaningful molecule representations, highlighting the strong capacity in molecule feature representation learning. We demonstrate that MechRetro outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches for retrosynthetic prediction with a large margin on large-scale benchmark datasets. Extending MechRetro to the multi-step retrosynthesis analysis, we identify efficient synthetic routes via an interpretable reasoning mechanism, leading to a better understanding in the realm of knowledgeable synthetic chemists. We also showcase that MechRetro discovers a novel pathway for protokylol, along with energy scores for uncertainty assessment, broadening the applicability for practical scenarios. Overall, we expect MechRetro to provide meaningful insights for high-throughput automated organic synthesis in drug discovery.

papers.title: Application of Modern Intelligent Algorithms in Retrosynthesis Prediction
papers.abstract: In recent years, the rapid advancements in computer science have spurred the development of various cutting-edge intelligent algorithms. Among these, the transformer, which is built upon a multi-head attention mechanism, is one of the most prominent AI models. The advent of such algorithms has significantly advanced retrosynthesis prediction, though challenges remain in chemical interpretability and real-world deployment. Unlike traditional models, AI-based retrosynthesis prediction systems can automatically extract chemical knowledge from vast datasets to forecast retrosynthesis pathways. This review provides a comprehensive overview of modern intelligent algorithms applied to retrosynthesis prediction, with a particular focus on artificial intelligence techniques. We begin by discussing key deep learning models, then explore available chemical reaction datasets and molecular representations. The discussion extends to the latest state-of-the art in AI-assisted retrosynthesis models, including template-based, template-free, and semi-template-based approaches. Finally, we compare these models across various classifications, highlighting several challenges and limitations of current methods, and suggesting promising directions for future research.

papers.title: Enhancing diversity in language based models for single-step retrosynthesis
papers.abstract: Over the past four years, several research groups demonstrated the combination of domain-specific language representation with recent NLP architectures to accelerate innovation in a wide range of scientific fields. Chemistry is a great example. Among the various chemical challenges addressed with language models, retrosynthesis demonstrates some of the most distinctive successes and limitations. Single-step retrosynthesis, the task of identifying reactions able to decompose a complex molecule into simpler structures, can be cast as a translation problem, in which a text-based representation of the target molecule is converted into a sequence of possible precursors. A common issue is a lack of diversity in the proposed disconnection strategies. The suggested precursors typically fall in the same reaction family, which limits the exploration of the chemical space. We present a retrosynthesis Transformer model that increases the diversity of the predictions by prepending a classification token to the language representation of the target molecule. At inference, the use of these prompt tokens allows us to steer the model towards different kinds of disconnection strategies. We show that the diversity of the predictions improves consistently, which enables recursive synthesis tools to circumvent dead ends and consequently, suggests synthesis pathways for more complex molecules.

papers.title: Data-driven Chemical Reaction Prediction and Retrosynthesis
papers.abstract: The synthesis of organic compounds, which is central to many areas such as drug discovery, material synthesis and biomolecular chemistry, requires chemists to have years of knowledge and experience. The development of technologies with the potential to learn and support experts in the design of synthetic routes is a half-century-old challenge with an interesting revival in the last decade.
