Without the need for complex training strategies or latent feature-learning components, our approach significantly extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% when compared with existing latent-space approaches, while maintaining comparable performance on common video quality metrics. In addition, we conduct interpretability experiments to identify network regions that encode information useful to perform accurate estimations of PDE simulation parameters via probing models, and find that this generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters. This work serves as a platform for further attention-based spatiotemporal modeling of videos via a simple, parameter efficient, and interpretable approach.

papers.title: Formal Mechanistic Interpretability: Automated Circuit Discovery with Provable Guarantees
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated circuit discovery in neural networks with provable guarantees (input domain robustness, patching robustness, and minimality) instead of relying on heuristics or approximations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel algorithmic framework that leverages neural network verification to automatically discover circuits (subgraphs) in neural networks with provable guarantees of input robustness, patching robustness, and various notions of minimality.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes a principled foundation for provable circuit discovery by combining mechanistic interpretability with neural network verification, offering circuits with formal guarantees and paving the way for future research.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed algorithms yield circuits with provable robustness guarantees across continuous input and patching domains, unlike sampling-based methods which can fail under small perturbations.
Theoretical connections are established between different families of guarantees (input robustness, patching robustness, minimality), underpinned by properties like circuit monotonicity and a duality between circuits and blocking sets.
Experiments on standard vision models and datasets show that the provable methods achieve 100% certified robustness, while sampling-based baselines exhibit significantly lower robustness.
The framework enables a trade-off between computational cost and the strength of minimality guarantees (quasi-, local-, subset-, and cardinal-minimality) in the discovered circuits.
A siamese encoding technique is introduced to certify input and patching robustness properties using off-the-shelf neural network verifiers.
papers.abstract: *Automated circuit discovery* is a central tool in mechanistic interpretability for identifying the internal components of neural networks responsible for specific behaviors. While prior methods have made significant progress, they typically depend on heuristics or approximations and do not offer provable guarantees over continuous input domains for the resulting circuits. In this work, we leverage recent advances in neural network verification to propose a suite of automated algorithms that yield circuits with *provable guarantees*. We focus on three types of guarantees: (1) *input domain robustness*, ensuring the circuit agrees with the model across a continuous input region; (2) *robust patching*, certifying circuit alignment under continuous patching perturbations; and (3) *minimality*, formalizing and capturing a wide array of various notions of succinctness. Interestingly, we uncover a diverse set of novel theoretical connections among these three families of guarantees, with critical implications for the convergence of our algorithms. Finally, we conduct experiments with state-of-the-art verifiers on various vision models, showing that our algorithms yield circuits with substantially stronger robustness guarantees than standard circuit discovery methods, establishing a principled foundation for provable circuit discovery.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Position: Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in SAEs
papers.research_question: How can feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be achieved and measured to improve the reliability of mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and proposes the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to measure consistency. It shows that high consistency is achievable with appropriate architectural choices (e.g., TopK SAEs) and that high PW-MCC correlates with semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.conclusion: The paper calls for a community-wide shift towards valuing and systematically measuring feature consistency in SAEs for cumulative progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
High feature consistency (PW-MCC ≈ 0.80) is achievable with TopK SAEs on real-world LLM activations.
PW-MCC reliably tracks ground-truth feature recovery (GT-MCC) in synthetic experiments.
Feature consistency is frequency-dependent: more frequent features are learned more consistently.
Different SAE architectures yield different levels of consistency, with TopK SAEs performing best.
High PW-MCC scores correlate strongly with the semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.limitation:
The focus is on SAEs, and other interpretability methods may have different consistency challenges.
The study uses a specific metric (PW-MCC) for a specific notion of consistency (strong feature consistency).
The real-world experiments are limited to two base models and one dataset.
The automated interpretation pipeline has its own limitations.
future_direction: Extending consistency analysis to other interpretability methods beyond SAEs.
Developing more nuanced metrics for consistency that go beyond strong feature consistency.
Investigating the relationship between consistency and downstream task performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a prominent tool in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for decomposing neural network activations into interpretable features. However, the aspiration to identify a canonical set of features is challenged by the observed inconsistency of learned SAE features across different training runs, undermining the reliability and efficiency of MI research. This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in SAEs -- the reliable convergence to equivalent feature sets across independent runs. We propose using the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to operationalize consistency and demonstrate that high levels are achievable (0.80 for TopK SAEs on LLM activations) with appropriate architectural choices. Our contributions include detailing the benefits of prioritizing consistency; providing theoretical grounding and synthetic validation using a model organism, which verifies PW-MCC as a reliable proxy for ground-truth recovery; and extending these findings to real-world LLM data, where high feature consistency strongly correlates with the semantic similarity of learned feature explanations. We call for a community-wide shift towards systematically measuring feature consistency to foster robust cumulative progress in MI.

papers.title: Opening the AI black box: program synthesis via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability be automated to distill learned algorithms from neural networks into Python code?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MIPS, a fully automated method that distills learned algorithms from RNNs into Python code via mechanistic interpretability, complementing LLMs like GPT-4.
papers.conclusion: MIPS is a promising step towards automated mechanistic interpretability and can complement large language models in program synthesis, offering a path to more interpretable and trustworthy machine-learned models.
papers.key_findings:
MIPS solves 32 out of 62 algorithmic tasks, including 13 that GPT-4 Turbo does not solve.
MIPS can automatically discover integer and Boolean representations in RNN hidden states.
The method converts trained RNNs into finite state machines and then synthesizes Python code via symbolic regression.
MIPS does not rely on human training data such as code from GitHub.
The method demonstrates the feasibility of automated mechanistic interpretability for program synthesis.
papers.limitation:
Noise and non-linearity in the RNN can cause the integer autoencoder to fail, preventing symbolic regression.
The method assumes the RNN is a finite-state machine and may fail when continuous variables are used for computation.
future_direction: Scaling up the approach to larger models.
Handling continuous variables in the learned representations.
Improving robustness to noise and non-linearity.
papers.abstract: We present MIPS, a novel method for program synthesis based on automated mechanistic interpretability of neural networks trained to perform the desired task, auto-distilling the learned algorithm into Python code. We test MIPS on a benchmark of 62 algorithmic tasks that can be learned by an RNN and find it highly complementary to GPT-4: MIPS solves 32 of them, including 13 that are not solved by GPT-4 (which also solves 30). MIPS uses an integer autoencoder to convert the RNN into a finite state machine, then applies Boolean or integer symbolic regression to capture the learned algorithm. As opposed to large language models, this program synthesis technique makes no use of (and is therefore not limited by) human training data such as algorithms and code from GitHub. We discuss opportunities and challenges for scaling up this approach to make machine-learned models more interpretable and trustworthy.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: Causal Intervention Framework for Variational Auto Encoder Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how Causal Effect Strength (CES) relates to traditional disentanglement metrics across VAE architectures, the effectiveness of disentanglement penalties based on factor count and latent dimensionality, whether causal metrics can reveal mechanistic differences not captured by traditional metrics, and how continuous interventions behave on discrete latent representations.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the first multi-level causal intervention framework for mechanistic interpretability of VAEs, with new metrics (CES, specificity, modularity), and empirically reveals key findings like the CES-DCI trade-off and β-VAE capacity bottleneck.
papers.conclusion: The framework and metrics advance mechanistic understanding of VAEs, revealing fundamental trade-offs and dataset-dependent optimality, with implications for model design and evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
A consistent within-dataset negative correlation between Causal Effect Strength (CES) and DCI disentanglement, termed the CES-DCI trade-off.
The KL reweighting mechanism of β-VAE causes a capacity bottleneck when generative factors approach latent dimensionality, degrading disentanglement on complex datasets.
No single VAE architecture is best across all datasets; optimal choice depends on dataset structure.
Continuous intervention metrics like CES yield near-zero values for discrete latent spaces (VQ-VAE), highlighting a limitation.
Causal intervention metrics provide mechanistic insights not captured by traditional disentanglement metrics.
papers.limitation:
DCI metric numerical instability due to dead latent dimensions producing infinite values.
FactorVAE hyperparameter interaction with batch size may underestimate disentanglement ability.
Training duration of 30 epochs may not ensure full convergence for all models.
Fixed latent dimensionality of 10 may affect capacity bottleneck conclusions.
CES metric combines magnitude and spatial extent, lacking finer decomposition.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other generative architectures like diffusion models and normalizing flows.
Developing discrete-native interpretability tools for quantized generative models.
Investigating how latent dimensionality interacts with disentanglement penalties.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability of deep learning models has emerged as a crucial research direction for understanding the functioning of neural networks. While significant progress has been made in interpreting discriminative models like transformers, understanding generative models such as Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) remains challenging. This paper introduces a comprehensive causal intervention framework for mechanistic interpretability of VAEs. We develop techniques to identify and analyze "circuit motifs" in VAEs, examining how semantic factors are encoded, processed, and disentangled through the network layers. Our approach uses targeted interventions at different levels: input manipulations, latent space perturbations, activation patching, and causal mediation analysis. We apply our framework to both synthetic datasets with known causal relationships and standard disentanglement benchmarks. Results show that our interventions can successfully isolate functional circuits, map computational graphs to causal graphs of semantic factors, and distinguish between polysemantic and monosemantic units. Furthermore, we introduce metrics for causal effect strength, intervention specificity, and circuit modularity that quantify the interpretability of VAE components. Experimental results demonstrate clear differences between VAE variants, with FactorVAE achieving higher disentanglement scores (0.084) and effect strengths (mean 4.59) compared to standard VAE (0.064, 3.99) and Beta-VAE (0.051, 3.43). Our framework advances the mechanistic understanding of generative models and provides tools for more transparent and controllable VAE architectures.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: Evaluating Self-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graph Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we effectively evaluate graph self-supervised learning (GSSL) methods for molecular graph embeddings, given that their broad applicability complicates evaluation and current downstream datasets may not provide a complete picture?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MOLGRAPH EVAL, a benchmark for evaluating molecular graph embeddings from GSSL methods via a suite of probing tasks, revealing significant inconsistencies between inferences from existing downstream datasets and more nuanced probing.
papers.conclusion: MOLGRAPH EVAL provides a more comprehensive and nuanced evaluation of GSSL methods for molecular graphs, uncovering limitations of current evaluation methodologies that rely solely on downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
All GSSL methods improve molecular property prediction (MPP) over random initialization, but the performance gain varies with dataset size.
Rankings of GSSL methods differ between using fixed embeddings (probing) and fine-tuned embeddings, indicating probing alone is not a definitive indicator for fine-tuning performance.
Optimal pre-training hyperparameters for fixed and fine-tuned embeddings often differ, suggesting that probing fixed embeddings may not reflect true downstream performance after fine-tuning.
Randomly initialized embeddings outperform almost every GSSL method on node- and pair-level topological metrics, indicating GSSL methods are not universally better and random features can be useful for local geometry tasks.
Substructure detection performance correlates well with MPP performance, suggesting that GSSL methods' superiority in MPP may be attributed to their capacity for substructure awareness.
papers.limitation:
The benchmark is limited to the nine studied GSSL methods and the molecular datasets used; extending to more methods and datasets is needed for broader conclusions.
Potential ethical concerns include bias and fairness in the datasets, dual use for designing harmful substances, environmental impact of training, and privacy issues.
future_direction: Extend the benchmark to incorporate more GSSL methods and larger datasets (e.g., ZINC15).
Investigate why optimal pre-training configurations for probing and fine-tuning differ.
Explore the reasons behind the strong performance of randomly initialized embeddings on local topological metrics.
papers.abstract: Graph Self-Supervised Learning (GSSL) provides a robust pathway for acquiring embeddings without expert labelling, a capability that carries profound implications for molecular graphs due to the staggering number of potential molecules and the high cost of obtaining labels. However, GSSL methods are designed not for optimisation within a specific domain but rather for transferability across a variety of downstream tasks. This broad applicability complicates their evaluation. Addressing this challenge, we present "Molecular Graph Representation Evaluation" (MOLGRAPHEVAL), generating detailed profiles of molecular graph embeddings with interpretable and diversified attributes. MOLGRAPHEVAL offers a suite of probing tasks grouped into three categories: (i) generic graph, (ii) molecular substructure, and (iii) embedding space properties. By leveraging MOLGRAPHEVAL to benchmark existing GSSL methods against both current downstream datasets and our suite of tasks, we uncover significant inconsistencies between inferences drawn solely from existing datasets and those derived from more nuanced probing. These findings suggest that current evaluation methodologies fail to capture the entirety of the landscape.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GAR is challenging for existing LLMs, with performance dropping significantly for harder tasks and the compositionality gap increasing with model scale.
Attribution patching reveals core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different GAR tasks, including a truthfulness sub-circuit and an in-context learning sub-circuit.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of identified vital attention heads (e.g., predicting, pre-predicting, higher-order local, induction, and relating heads) significantly impacts task performance.
Two classes of higher-order relating heads (True and False heads) are identified whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks.
The activation patterns of the True/False heads generalize to other datasets (SNLI and GoT), indicating they encode information for truthfulness classification beyond GAR.
papers.limitation: The circuit discovery is done manually without using automatic circuit discovery methods, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and more complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks, and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play fundamental roles in CRR across various models and tasks.

papers.title: A Chain Graph Interpretation of Real-World Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can neural networks be interpreted as chain graphs (probabilistic graphical models) with feed-forward as approximate probabilistic inference, and what insights or new methods does this interpretation provide?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a chain graph interpretation of neural networks, identifying them as layered chain graphs and feed-forward as approximate probabilistic inference, providing theoretical support for existing designs and deriving new methods like partially collapsed feed-forward.
papers.conclusion: The chain graph interpretation is a promising theoretical framework that deepens understanding of neural networks, provides coherent support for existing designs, and enables derivation of new deep learning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can be rigorously interpreted as layered chain graphs, with feed-forward corresponding to approximate probabilistic inference using linear approximations.
The chain graph interpretation provides theoretical support for residual blocks (as refinement modules), recurrent neural networks (with insights on IndRNN), and dropout (via auxiliary Bernoulli variables).
The interpretation leads to a novel stochastic inference method called partially collapsed feed-forward (PCFF), which mixes deterministic feed-forward and stochastic sampling.
Empirical experiments show that PCFF is an effective stochastic regularization method, sometimes outperforming dropout, and works across various architectures (dense nets, ResNet, IndRNN).
The linear approximation used in feed-forward is coarse and accurate only for small weights, which may explain neural networks' vulnerability to adversarial samples.
papers.limitation:
The chain graph interpretation may not be sufficient to capture the full essence of neural networks and might not cover all important network designs.
The linear approximations used to derive feed-forward are coarse and only accurate for small pairwise weights, potentially leading to errors such as vulnerability to adversarial samples.
future_direction: Investigate whether the chain graph interpretation is sufficient to capture the full essence of neural networks.
Find chain graph interpretations for other important network designs or develop interpretable alternatives with comparable performance.
Derive other new deep learning models and procedures based on the chain graph framework.
papers.abstract: The last decade has witnessed a boom of deep learning research and applications achieving state-of-the-art results in various domains. However, most advances have been established empirically, and their theoretical analysis remains lacking. One major issue is that our current interpretation of neural networks (NNs) as function approximators is too generic to support in-depth analysis. In this paper, we remedy this by proposing an alternative interpretation that identifies NNs as chain graphs (CGs) and feed-forward as an approximate inference procedure. The CG interpretation specifies the nature of each NN component within the rich theoretical framework of probabilistic graphical models, while at the same time remains general enough to cover real-world NNs with arbitrary depth, multi-branching and varied activations, as well as common structures including convolution / recurrent layers, residual block and dropout. We demonstrate with concrete examples that the CG interpretation can provide novel theoretical support and insights for various NN techniques, as well as derive new deep learning approaches such as the concept of partially collapsed feed-forward inference. It is thus a promising framework that deepens our understanding of neural networks and provides a coherent theoretical formulation for future deep learning research.

papers.title: On the Mechanistic Interpretability of Neural Networks for Causality in Bio-statistics
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability techniques be transposed to bio-statistics, and how effective are they?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability tools can be leveraged to probe and validate internal representations learned by neural networks for causal inference, discover and visualize computational pathways for confounders and treatments, and compare learned mechanisms across model types.
papers.abstract: Interpretable insights from predictive models remain critical in bio-statistics, particularly when assessing causality, where classical statistical and machine learning methods often provide inherent clarity. While Neural Networks (NNs) offer powerful capabilities for modeling complex biological data, their traditional "black-box" nature presents challenges for validation and trust in high-stakes health applications. Recent advances in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aim to decipher the internal computations learned by these networks. This work investigates the application of MI techniques to NNs within the context of causal inference for bio-statistics. We demonstrate that MI tools can be leveraged to: (1) probe and validate the internal representations learned by NNs, such as those estimating nuisance functions in frameworks like Targeted Minimum Loss-based Estimation (TMLE); (2) discover and visualize the distinct computational pathways employed by the network to process different types of inputs, potentially revealing how confounders and treatments are handled; and (3) provide methodologies for comparing the learned mechanisms and extracted insights across statistical, machine learning, and NN models, fostering a deeper understanding of their respective strengths and weaknesses for causal bio-statistical analysis.

papers.title: Disentangling Neuron Representations with Concept Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we find meaningful directions (concept vectors) in activation space that correspond to distinct features, starting from polysemantic neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors that represent distinct features, allowing for fine-grained concept separation controlled by a distance threshold.
papers.conclusion: Exploring directions in activation space (concept vectors) instead of individual neurons can lead to finding coherent fundamental units, bridging mechanistic interpretability and concept discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into concept vectors that are linear combinations of neurons.
The concept vectors encode coherent, human-understandable features, as validated by human experiments.
The method can separate fine-grained concepts (e.g., underwater scenes vs. scuba divers) by adjusting a distance threshold.
The latent space representations have higher similarity with the discovered concept vectors than with the neuron directions.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the data used to generate clusters.
All experiments were performed on image data, which may limit generalizability to other data types.
future_direction: Generalizing the method to other data types such as language and tabular data.
Looking at other starting candidates for concepts besides neurons.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how models store representations by breaking down neural networks into interpretable units. However, the occurrence of polysemantic neurons, or neurons that respond to multiple unrelated features, makes interpreting individual neurons challenging. This has led to the search for meaningful vectors, known as concept vectors, in activation space instead of individual neurons. The main contribution of this paper is a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors encapsulating distinct features. Our method can search for fine-grained concepts according to the user’s desired level of concept separation. The analysis shows that polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into directions consisting of linear combinations of neurons. Our evaluations show that the concept vectors found encode coherent, human-understandable features.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Combining Causal Models for More Accurate Abstractions of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we improve the faithfulness of causal abstractions of neural networks by combining multiple high-level causal models to allow for different computational states depending on the input?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for combining causal models to create more faithful abstractions of neural networks, enabling different computational states for different inputs and demonstrating a trade-off between hypothesis strength and faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: Combining causal models enables more nuanced interpretations of neural computation, providing stronger interpretability hypotheses while maintaining high faithfulness, as demonstrated on arithmetic and boolean logic tasks with GPT 2-small.
papers.key_findings:
Combined causal models provide stronger interpretability hypotheses at high faithfulness levels (0.9-1.0 IIA) compared to individual models.
There is a trade-off between faithfulness (measured by Interchange Intervention Accuracy) and hypothesis strength (proportion of inputs assigned to non-trivial models).
In GPT 2-small fine-tuned on arithmetic and boolean tasks, the model does not transition discretely between computational states; combined models can capture this nuance.
The method allows modulation between strength and faithfulness, providing the most accurate combination of models given a faithfulness level.
Early layers of GPT 2-small represent input variables separately, while later layers represent summed quantities, with a gradual transition in intermediate layers.
papers.limitation: Experiments are conducted on toy tasks (arithmetic and boolean logic) for clear analysis and validation.
future_direction: Extend the framework to more complex tasks.
Integrate with other mechanistic interpretability methods.
Enhance with more sophisticated optimization objectives for constructing input space partitions.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse engineer neural networks by uncovering which high-level algorithms they implement. Causal abstraction provides a precise notion of when a network implements an algorithm, i.e., a causal model of the network contains low-level features that realize the high-level variables in a causal model of the algorithm. A typical problem in practical settings is that the algorithm is not an entirely faithful abstraction of the network, meaning it only partially captures the true reasoning process of a model. We propose a solution where we combine different simple high-level models to produce a more faithful representation of the network. Through learning this combination, we can model neural networks as being in different computational states depending on the input provided, which we show is more accurate to GPT 2-small fine-tuned on two toy tasks. We observe a trade-off between the strength of an interpretability hypothesis, which we define in terms of the number of inputs explained by the high-level models, and its faithfulness, which we define as the interchange intervention accuracy. Our method allows us to modulate between the two, providing the most accurate combination of models that describe the behavior of a neural network given a faithfulness level.

papers.title: Explaining AI through mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we achieve holistic explanations of AI systems that reveal their functional organization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that XAI should adopt mechanistic interpretability (MI) to uncover the functional organization of trained AI systems, which is necessary for holistic explanations and meeting societal desiderata such as safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability is a promising approach for achieving holistic explanations of AI systems and should be integrated into XAI research to meet important societal desiderata.
papers.key_findings:
Current XAI methods, while useful in specific contexts, fail to provide holistic explanations of how AI systems work as a whole.
Mechanistic interpretability, which applies discovery strategies from the life sciences, can reveal the functional organization of AI systems.
The case of Distill demonstrates that MI can successfully identify circuits (like curve detectors) and explain model behavior.
MI enables better prediction and control of AI systems, contributing to safety and trust.
MI is complementary to traditional XAI and should be accommodated in XAI research.
papers.limitation:
The complexity of large models makes mechanistic interpretability hopeless.
MI may be too resource-intensive.
MI may be unnecessary for many applications.
MI may be prone to overfitting and cherry-picking.
MI may be limited by the entanglement of representations in neural networks.
MI may be limited by the fact that neural networks are not modular.
papers.abstract: Abstract Recent work in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) attempts to render opaque AI systems understandable through a divide-and-conquer strategy. However, this fails to illuminate how trained AI systems work as a whole . Precisely this kind of functional understanding is needed, though, to satisfy important societal desiderata such as safety. To remedy this situation, we argue, AI researchers should seek mechanistic interpretability , viz. apply coordinated discovery strategies familiar from the life sciences to uncover the functional organisation of complex AI systems. Additionally, theorists should accommodate for the unique costs and benefits of such strategies in their portrayals of XAI research.

papers.title: Position-aware Automatic Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate positional information into automatic circuit discovery for language models to address limitations of position-agnostic methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces position-aware circuit discovery (PEAP) and dataset schemas to enable fully automated discovery of position-sensitive circuits, achieving better faithfulness than position-agnostic methods.
papers.conclusion: Position-aware circuit discovery and schemas improve circuit faithfulness and enable automated analysis of variable-length inputs, providing a more precise foundation for mechanistic explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Position-aware circuits are smaller and more faithful than position-agnostic circuits.
Automatically generated schemas (with or without saliency masks) yield circuits comparable to those from human-designed schemas.
The proposed method handles variable-length inputs via schemas, enabling circuit discovery in more naturalistic settings.
papers.limitation:
Schemas assume sequential order of spans, which may not hold for all datasets.
The schema generation and application pipeline may not always produce valid schemas for all examples.
future_direction: Relax the sequential order assumption in schemas to support greater variation across examples.
Investigate the components in the circuit for the Winobias task to understand the balance between task-relevant and bias-inducing factors.

papers.title: ACES-GNN: can graph neural network learn to explain activity cliffs?
papers.research_question: Can Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) be trained to provide better explanations for activity cliffs (structurally similar molecules with significant potency differences) while also improving prediction accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the ACES-GNN framework, which integrates explanation supervision for activity cliffs into GNN training, improving both predictive accuracy and the interpretability of molecular structure-property relationships.
papers.conclusion: ACES-GNN represents a promising direction for improving both the predictivity and interpretability of GNN models in QSAR applications, with the potential to accelerate lead optimization in drug discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ACES-GNN improves explainability (global direction) on 28 out of 30 datasets compared to unsupervised GNNs.
ACES-GNN improves prediction accuracy for activity cliff molecules, reducing RMSE_cliff.
A positive correlation exists between the improvement in prediction accuracy and the improvement in explanation quality.
The ACES framework is effective across different GNN backbones (MPNN, GIN, GAT).
Explanation supervision helps the model focus on uncommon substructures critical for activity cliffs, aligning attributions with chemist-friendly interpretations.
papers.limitation:
The ground-truth coloring relies on a fixed definition for activity cliff molecules, and some uncommon substructures between pairs may not be causative for potency changes.
The current GNN backbone does not outperform the Random Forest + ECFP combination in predictive accuracy or attribution quality across all datasets.
The validation process prioritizes minimizing RMSE during training rather than optimizing the explainability metric, so not all attributions after supervision achieve higher global direction accuracy.
future_direction: Incorporate geometric information into GNNs for further improvement.
Explore alternative gradient-based explanation techniques, such as expected gradients, to reduce potential biases.
Develop methods to identify true causal substructures in activity cliffs, enhancing explanation evaluation and guidance.
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have revolutionized molecular property prediction by leveraging graph-based representations, yet their opaque decision-making processes hinder broader adoption in drug discovery. This study introduces the Activity-Cliff-Explanation-Supervised GNN (ACES-GNN) framework, designed to simultaneously improve predictive accuracy and interpretability by integrating explanation supervision for activity cliffs (ACs) into GNN training. ACs, defined by structurally similar molecules with significant potency differences, pose challenges for traditional models due to their reliance on shared structural features. By aligning model attributions with chemist-friendly interpretations, the ACES-GNN framework bridges the gap between prediction and explanation. Validated across 30 pharmacological targets, ACES-GNN consistently enhances both predictive accuracy and attribution quality for ACs compared to unsupervised GNNs. Our results demonstrate a positive correlation between improved predictions and accurate explanations, offering a robust and adaptable framework to better understand and interpret ACs. This work underscores the potential of explanation-guided learning to advance interpretable artificial intelligence in molecular modeling and drug discovery.

papers.title: Localized Definitions and Distributed Reasoning: A Proof-of-Concept Mechanistic Interpretability Study via Activation Patching
papers.research_question: How is knowledge representation localized in fine-tuned language models, and how does it vary with task complexity?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that factual knowledge is localized while associative knowledge is distributed in fine-tuned models, and introduces CLAP for causal layer attribution.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is localized while associative reasoning depends on distributed intermediate representations, highlighting task-dependent knowledge organization.
papers.key_findings:
Patching the first feedforward layer recovered 56% of correct preference for associative knowledge, indicating distributed representations.
Patching the final output layer completely restored accuracy (100% recovery) for definitional knowledge, indicating localized representation.
Minimal recovery from convolutional layer patching (13.6%) suggests low-level features contribute marginally to high-level reasoning.
Statistical analysis confirmed significant layer-specific effects (p<0.01).
Editing efficacy depends on task type, with factual knowledge more localized and associative knowledge depending on distributed representations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis focused exclusively on PubMed epilepsy-related abstracts, potentially limiting generalizability to broader knowledge tasks.
Activation patching may generate false positives due to indirect causal pathways.
Exclusive focus on GPT-2 leaves open questions about scalability to other architectures.
future_direction: Cross-domain comparisons to better understand task-dependent representation patterns.
Methodological integration to improve efficiency.
Extensions to multimodal models where knowledge distribution mechanisms may differ significantly.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the localization of knowledge representation in fine-tuned GPT-2 models using Causal Layer Attribution via Activation Patching (CLAP), a method that identifies critical neural layers responsible for correct answer generation. The model was fine-tuned on 9,958 PubMed abstracts (epilepsy: 20,595 mentions, EEG: 11,674 mentions, seizure: 13,921 mentions) using two configurations with validation loss monitoring for early stopping. CLAP involved (1) caching clean (correct answer) and corrupted (incorrect answer) activations, (2) computing logit difference to quantify model preference, and (3) patching corrupted activations with clean ones to assess recovery. Results revealed three findings: First, patching the first feedforward layer recovered 56% of correct preference, demonstrating that associative knowledge is distributed across multiple layers. Second, patching the final output layer completely restored accuracy (100% recovery), indicating that definitional knowledge is localised. The stronger clean logit difference for definitional questions further supports this localized representation. Third, minimal recovery from convolutional layer patching (13.6%) suggests low-level features contribute marginally to high-level reasoning. Statistical analysis confirmed significant layer-specific effects (p<0.01). These findings demonstrate that factual knowledge is more localized and associative knowledge depends on distributed representations. We also showed that editing efficacy depends on task type. Our findings not only reconcile conflicting observations about localization in model editing but also emphasize on using task-adaptive techniques for reliable, interpretable updates.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs Philosophy
papers.research_question: How can philosophy contribute to mechanistic interpretability? The paper investigates three open problems in MI and how philosophy can help.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that mechanistic interpretability needs philosophy to clarify its concepts, refine its methods, and assess the epistemic and ethical stakes of interpreting AI systems.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that philosophy is deeply relevant to mechanistic interpretability and invites deeper interdisciplinary collaboration that is technically informed and philosophically grounded.
papers.key_findings:
Philosophy can help in decomposing networks into interpretable parts by providing conceptual tools from mechanistic explanation and challenging the assumption of a single true decomposition.
Philosophy can clarify the concept of 'features' in AI systems by distinguishing between vehicles and content of representations, refining experimental approaches, and suggesting new lines of investigation.
Philosophy can help in detecting deceptive behavior by clarifying concepts like lying and deception, guiding the search for AI beliefs, and drawing ethical and normative boundaries.
future_direction: Deeper interdisciplinary collaboration between philosophy and mechanistic interpretability.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to explain how neural networks work by uncovering their underlying causal mechanisms. As the field grows in influence, it is increasingly important to examine not just models themselves, but the assumptions, concepts and explanatory strategies implicit in MI research. We argue that mechanistic interpretability needs philosophy: not as an afterthought, but as an ongoing partner in clarifying its concepts, refining its methods, and assessing the epistemic and ethical stakes of interpreting AI systems. Taking three open problems from the MI literature as examples, this position paper illustrates the value philosophy can add to MI research, and outlines a path toward deeper interdisciplinary dialogue.

papers.title: Tensor Product Decomposition Networks: Uncovering Representations of Structure Learned by Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode compositional symbolic structure in their vector representations, and do they use tensor product representations?
papers.core_contribution: TPDNs show that RNNs can learn structured representations similar to tensor product representations for artificial tasks, but for real-world NLP tasks, representations are less structured, approximated by bag-of-words, suggesting training tasks may not induce robust structural representations.
papers.conclusion: RNNs trained on structure-sensitive tasks learn representations well approximated by tensor-product representations, but sentence encoders for NLP tasks show less structure, approximated by bag-of-words.
papers.key_findings:
TPDNs can closely approximate RNN representations for digit sequence copying tasks, indicating structured encoding.
Linear RNNs use bidirectional role schemes, while tree RNNs use tree position roles for representation.
For natural language processing models like InferSent and Skip-thought, representations are well approximated by bag-of-words, showing limited structure.
The nature of learned representations is related to the RNN's structure and the training task.
Training tasks influence whether networks discover structured or unstructured representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce an analysis technique for understanding compositional structure present in the vector representations used by neural networks. The inner workings of neural networks are notoriously difficult to understand, and in particular it is far from clear how they manage to perform remarkably well on tasks that depend on compositional structure even though they use continuous vector representations with no obvious compositional structure. Using our analysis technique, we show that the representations of these models can be closely approximated by Tensor Product Representations, a type of interpretable structure that lends significant insight into the workings of these hard-to-interpret models.

papers.title: Sparse Reward Subsystem in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states analogous to the biological reward subsystem, and what are its properties?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states, consisting of value neurons that encode state value and dopamine neurons that encode reward prediction error, and shows their critical role in reasoning and their robustness across models and tasks.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a sparse reward subsystem analogous to the biological reward subsystem, which is consistent across tasks, layers, model scales, and architectures, and has potential applications.
papers.key_findings:
Value neurons exist in LLM hidden states and can predict the value of the current state using only a small fraction of neurons.
Ablating even 1% of value neurons severely impairs reasoning performance, while random ablation does not.
Value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, layers, and architectural designs.
Value neurons are transferable across different datasets and across models fine-tuned from the same base model.
Dopamine neurons exist and encode reward prediction error, with activation patterns correlating with positive and negative surprises.
papers.limitation: Dopamine neurons are demonstrated primarily through case studies rather than quantitative metrics.
future_direction: Further explore applications of the reward subsystem for detecting and guiding LLM generation and reasoning.
Develop quantitative metrics for measuring dopamine neurons.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify a sparse reward subsystem within the hidden states of Large Language Models (LLMs), drawing an analogy to the biological reward subsystem in the human brain. We demonstrate that this subsystem contains value neurons that represent the model's internal expectation of state value, and through intervention experiments, we establish the importance of these neurons for reasoning. Our experiments reveal that these value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, and architectures; furthermore, they exhibit significant transferability across different datasets and models fine-tuned from the same base model. By examining cases where value predictions and actual rewards diverge, we identify dopamine neurons within the reward subsystem which encode reward prediction errors (RPE). These neurons exhibit high activation when the reward is higher than expected and low activation when the reward is lower than expected.

papers.title: Understanding the Failure Modes of Transformers through the Lens of Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the failure modes of transformers, and how can they be understood through the lens of graph neural network theory?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical understanding of transformer failure modes (over-smoothing, over-squashing, under-reaching) through the lens of GNN theory, and interprets existing ad-hoc solutions (like pause tokens and differential transformer) within this framework.
papers.conclusion: Theoretical issues like over-smoothing and over-squashing limit transformer improvement, and existing solutions are often ad-hoc; GNN theory provides a grounded perspective to guide future research.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers suffer from over-smoothing (rank collapse) due to repeated information mixing, similar to GNNs.
The causal mask in decoder-only transformers creates a position bias, leading to attention sinks and over-squashing of later tokens (the runway problem).
Existing solutions like pause tokens and the differential transformer can be interpreted as mitigating over-smoothing and the runway problem.
GNN theory offers a unified framework to understand transformer failure modes and explain why certain intuitive fixes work.
papers.abstract: Transformers and more specifically decoder-only transformers dominate modern LLM architectures. While they have shown to work exceptionally well, they are not without issues, resulting in surprising failure modes and predictably asymmetric performance degradation. This article is a study of many of these observed failure modes of transformers through the lens of graph neural network (GNN) theory. We first make the case that much of deep learning, including transformers, is about learnable information mixing and propagation. This makes the study of model failure modes a study of bottlenecks in information propagation. This naturally leads to GNN theory, where there is already a rich literature on information propagation bottlenecks and theoretical failure modes of models. We then make the case that many issues faced by GNNs are also experienced by transformers. In addition, we analyze how the causal nature of decoder-only transformers create interesting geometric properties in information propagation, resulting in predictable and potentially devastating failure modes. Finally, we observe that existing solutions in transformer research tend to be ad-hoc and driven by intuition rather than grounded theoretical motivation. As such, we unify many such solutions under a more theoretical perspective, providing insight into why they work, what problem they are actually solving, and how they can be further improved to target specific failure modes of transformers. Overall, this article is an attempt to bridge the gap between observed failure modes in transformers and a general lack of theoretical understanding of them in this space.

papers.title: Modular addition without black-boxes: Compressing explanations of MLPs that compute numerical integration
papers.research_question: How can we compress nonlinear feature-maps (MLP layers) in neural networks to understand their internal algorithms? The paper presents a case study on modular addition models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a method to compress nonlinear feature-maps in MLP layers by interpreting them as performing numerical integration, demonstrated on modular addition models.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a first case study in rigorously compressing nonlinear feature-maps, demonstrating that interpreting feature-maps reveals additional insight about model mechanisms and hopes to inspire further study.
papers.key_findings:
The MLP in modular addition models can be interpreted as performing numerical integration to double the frequency of input representations.
Neurons have primary and secondary frequencies, with output phases approximately double the input phases.
Secondary frequencies compensate for weaknesses in the 'pizza' algorithm when |cos(k(a-b)/2)| is small.
Non-vacuous bounds on MLP outputs can be derived in time linear in the number of parameters.
The infinite-width lens allows turning post-activation matrix multiplications into approximate integrals for analysis.
papers.limitation: The error bounds derived are not tight because the understanding of numerical integration in the network is incomplete.
future_direction: Developing automated tools for approximating and interpreting neural networks using low-rank approximations like Fourier expansion.
Improving error bounds and parameterizations of the model to account for all components.
papers.abstract: The goal of mechanistic interpretability is discovering simpler, low-rank algorithms implemented by models. While we can compress activations into features, compressing nonlinear feature-maps -- like MLP layers -- is an open problem. In this work, we present the first case study in rigorously compressing nonlinear feature-maps, which are the leading asymptotic bottleneck to compressing small transformer models. We work in the classic setting of the modular addition models, and target a non-vacuous bound on the behaviour of the ReLU MLP in time linear in the parameter-count of the circuit. To study the ReLU MLP analytically, we use the infinite-width lens, which turns post-activation matrix multiplications into approximate integrals. We discover a novel interpretation of} the MLP layer in one-layer transformers implementing the ``pizza'' algorithm: the MLP can be understood as evaluating a quadrature scheme, where each neuron computes the area of a rectangle under the curve of a trigonometric integral identity. Our code is available at https://tinyurl.com/mod-add-integration.

papers.title: Decomposition of Small Transformer Models
papers.research_question: Can Stochastic Parameter Decomposition (SPD) be extended to Transformer models to decompose their weights into interpretable, causally relevant subcomponents?
papers.core_contribution: Extends Stochastic Parameter Decomposition (SPD) to Transformer models by proposing a causal importance function for sequential data and a new loss function, demonstrating that SPD can recover interpretable parameter-space mechanisms in both a toy induction-head model and GPT-2-small.
papers.conclusion: Parameter decomposition can surface semantically specific mechanisms in Transformers, and SPD yields narrow, causally relevant directions that act as clean handles for mechanistic interventions.
papers.key_findings:
SPD successfully decomposes a toy induction-head model and recovers the expected 2-step copy circuit.
Applying SPD to GPT-2-small locates subcomponents corresponding to interpretable concepts like 'golf' and 'basketball'.
Ablating the recovered rank-1 slices selectively reduces the probability of the targeted fact (e.g., 'golf' for Tiger Woods) while leaving unrelated examples largely unaffected.
The method achieves a 99% size reduction in active subcomponents for the GPT-2-small fact examples compared to the full model.
Facts like athlete-sport associations can originate as early as the first MLP layer and propagate through the network.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are restricted to small-scale models, leaving open questions about scalability to larger architectures.
The causal importance parameterisation introduces additional computational overhead.
Evaluation is qualitative and task-specific, so further benchmarks are needed to establish generality across architectures and tasks.
Difficulty in establishing ground truth even for small, toy Transformers.
future_direction: Extend this work to larger models.
Improve the definition of causal importance for computations with feature interactions.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that decomposing models in parameter space may yield clean handles for analysis and intervention. Previous methods have demonstrated successful applications on a wide range of toy models, but the gap to "real models" has not yet been bridged. In this work, we extend Stochastic Parameter Decomposition (SPD) to Transformer models, proposing an updated causal importance function suited for sequential data and a new loss function. We demonstrate that SPD can successfully decompose a toy induction-head model and recover the expected 2-step circuit. We also show that applying SPD to GPT-2-small can successfully locate subcomponents corresponding to interpretable concepts like "golf" and "basketball". These results take the first step in the direction of extending SPD to modern models, and show that we can use the method to surface interpretable parameter-space mechanisms.

papers.title: Transformers learn factored representations
papers.research_question: Do transformers learn to factor their world into parts from next-token prediction, and why would they have an inductive bias for factored representations?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers learn to factor their world into parts, representing each factor in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream, and show an inductive bias toward factored representations even when it is lossy.
papers.conclusion: Transformers decompose the world into parts and represent them in orthogonal subspaces due to an inductive bias from next-token prediction, suggesting interpretable low-dimensional structure may persist in models trained on complex data.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn factored representations in orthogonal subspaces when data has conditionally independent factors.
The dimensionality of activations collapses to the linearly growing factored prediction, not the exponentially growing joint representation.
Factor subspaces become approximately orthogonal over training, as measured by subspace overlap and dimensionality additivity.
Factoring begins at the token embedding layer, with the embedding matrix developing low-rank structure corresponding to factor subspaces.
Transformers exhibit an inductive bias toward factored representations, learning them early even when data is not perfectly factorable, sacrificing fidelity for dimensional efficiency.
papers.limitation: Experiments are conducted on synthetic data with known latent structure, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Investigate whether differences in factorization behavior between transformers, RNNs, and LSTMs are due to training dynamics or inductive bias.
papers.abstract: Transformers pretrained via next token prediction learn to factor their world into parts, representing these factors in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream. We formalize two representational hypotheses: (1) a representation in the product space of all factors, whose dimension grows exponentially with the number of parts, or (2) a factored representation in orthogonal subspaces, whose dimension grows linearly. The factored representation is lossless when factors are conditionally independent, but sacrifices predictive fidelity otherwise, creating a tradeoff between dimensional efficiency and accuracy. We derive precise predictions about the geometric structure of activations for each, including the number of subspaces, their dimensionality, and the arrangement of context embeddings within them. We test between these hypotheses on transformers trained on synthetic processes with known latent structure. Models learn factored representations when factors are conditionally independent, and continue to favor them early in training even when noise or hidden dependencies undermine conditional independence, reflecting an inductive bias toward factoring at the cost of fidelity. This provides a principled explanation for why transformers decompose the world into parts, and suggests that interpretable low dimensional structure may persist even in models trained on complex data.

papers.title: APP: Accelerated Path Patching with Task-Specific Pruning
papers.research_question: Can pruning be used for circuit discovery, and how can we accelerate path patching by reducing the search space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid method that uses Contrastive-FLAP pruning to reduce the search space for circuit discovery, achieving significant speedups while recovering minimal circuits with performance comparable to standard path patching.
papers.conclusion: APP provides a scalable preprocessing step for circuit discovery, making mechanistic interpretability more efficient and practical for large models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning alone cannot recover minimal circuits; circuits found by pruning are larger than those found by path patching.
Contrastive-FLAP, a novel pruning method, better preserves task-specific attention heads compared to vanilla FLAP.
APP reduces the search space for circuit discovery by an average of 56%, leading to speedups of 59.63%-93.27% compared to standard path patching.
Circuits discovered by APP have substantial overlap and similar performance to those found by standard path patching.
APP enables circuit discovery to scale to larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) by reducing computational costs.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter search is limited by computational cost, especially for large models.
Trade-off between circuit size and performance requires researcher discretion.
APP focuses on attention heads and does not include MLP components, which may be important for some tasks.
The true positive rate of hybrid FLAP caps the ability to recover all heads in the circuit.
future_direction: Extending APP to other circuit discovery algorithms like ACDC.
Incorporating MLP components into the automated path patching method.
Studying whether circuits discovered in GPT-2 small translate to larger models.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery is a key step in many mechanistic interpretability pipelines. Current methods, such as Path Patching, are computationally expensive and have limited in-depth circuit analysis for smaller models. In this study, we propose Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid approach leveraging our novel contrastive attention head pruning method to drastically reduce the search space of circuit discovery methods. Our Contrastive-FLAP pruning algorithm uses techniques from causal mediation analysis to assign higher pruning scores to task-specific attention heads, leading to higher performing sparse models compared to traditional pruning techniques. Although Contrastive-FLAP is successful at preserving task-specific heads that existing pruning algorithms remove at low sparsity ratios, the circuits found by Contrastive-FLAP alone are too large to satisfy the minimality constraint required in circuit analysis. APP first applies Contrastive-FLAP to reduce the search space on required for circuit discovery algorithms by, on average, 56\%. Next, APP, applies traditional Path Patching on the remaining attention heads, leading to a speed up of 59.63\%-93.27\% compared to Path Patching applied to the dense model. Despite the substantial computational saving that APP provides, circuits obtained from APP exhibit substantial overlap and similar performance to previously established Path Patching circuits

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average.
